en: The Ornament of the Mahāyāna Sūtras. Om, homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. The First Chapter.

Knowing the meaning, he manifests that meaning through speech and pure words out of compassion for suffering beings, being absorbed in that very purpose for the sake of crossing over suffering. To those beings who travel upon it, he demonstrates the fivefold, unsurpassed, and coherent progression of the meaning of the Dharma according to the method taught in the Supreme Vehicle.
Like gold that has been fashioned, like a lotus in full bloom, like well-prepared food being enjoyed by those afflicted by hunger,
like a fine letter deciphered, or like a casket of jewels opened— this Dharma, when revealed here, bestows supreme joy.
Just as a reflection endowed with the qualities of its natural form and ornaments produces exceptional joy in people by virtue of being seen when it appears in a mirror,
so too the Dharma, though already possessed of the qualities of its well-spoken nature, generates a distinguished satisfaction among the virtuous here when its meaning is constantly analyzed.
Just as a medicine may be pungent to the smell yet sweet in taste, so too the Dharma should be understood as being established in two ways: by way of the letter and by way of the meaning. (MSA 1.4)
This Dharma, vast, profound, and deep, is like a king difficult to propitiate;
yet when propitiated, it likewise becomes the bestower of the wealth of excellent qualities.
Just as a noble, priceless gem does not satisfy a person who lacks the power of discernment, so too this Dharma, through its very opposite, causes distress to the ignorant. MSA 1.6.

Because it was not prophesied at the beginning, because it arose simultaneously [with the Buddha], because it is beyond the sphere [of logic], because it is established [as such], because it does not exist in the presence or absence [of conditions], because it is the antidote, and because it is other than the literal word. // MSA 1.7 //
The Buddhas possess direct vision and are the protectors of the teaching;
since their knowledge is not obscured by pride, it is not appropriate for them to remain indifferent.
Because of deficiency, contradiction, lack of means, and likewise because of the absence of instruction, this which is called the Mahāyāna Dharma cannot be the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
Due to the inferiority of intention, instruction, application, support, and time, that which is inferior is indeed inferior. (MSA 1.10)
Because it is included within its own [scriptures], because it is seen in its own discipline (vinaya),
and because of its vastness and profundity, the nature of reality (dharmatā) is indeed not contradictory.

Reasoning is considered to be dependent, indeterminate, non-pervasive, conventional, subject to weariness, and based on the intellect of the foolish; therefore, that [Ultimate Truth] is not its object.
Because of its magnificence and its profundity, there is maturation and non-conceptuality;
therefore, the teaching of these two in this [sūtra] is the means for the unsurpassed [state]. (MSA 1.13)
Thus, groundless fear arises for those in the world, causing them to burn for a long duration because it produces a great mass of demerit.

One who lacks the spiritual lineage, who has bad friends, whose intellect is untrained, and who has not previously accumulated merit—falling away from this Dharma which is true—herein loses a great benefit. (MSA 1.14)

Because it is the absence of one thing in another, because of its supreme profundity, because of its conformity, because of the description of the manifold, and because of the connection with constant teaching through many doors;

because the meaning does not exist as it is described, and because the reality within the Blessed One is exceedingly profound— wise persons do not experience fear regarding this Dharma, due to their systematic investigation.
Relying first upon what has been heard, mental attention arises here;
from that mental attention, knowledge whose object is the meaning of reality arises.
From that, the attainment of the Dharma arises, and from that, wisdom is produced.
Since that [reality] is personally realized within oneself, how can there be a firm conviction when it does not exist? (MSA 1.16)

"I am not an enlightened one, nor an enlightened one who understands the profound; how could the profound be accessible through reasoning? Why would there be no liberation for those who know the profound meaning?"—this ground for fear is not logical. (MSA 1.17)

If one who is of inferior inclination, belonging to a very low disposition, and surrounded by inferior companions lacks faith in this Dharma so well-taught in its vastness and profundity, then [the superiority of the Mahāyāna] is established. (MSA 1.18)

For how can a fool, having attained the status of a wise person by following what he has heard, yet show contempt for what he has not heard—when there remains a vast and immeasurable variety of sacred learning? (MSA 1.19)
When the meaning is conceptualized according to the literal expression, one's own conviction leads to the loss of intelligence;
it casts aside the well-expounded nature [of the teaching], incurs harm, and becomes as if hostile toward the Dharma. (MSA 1.20)

Mental malice is by nature corrupt; it is indeed improper even regarding what is not heard correctly, let alone regarding a Dharma that has fallen into doubt. Therefore, equanimity alone is better, for it is faultless.
The first chapter, on the Establishment of the Mahāyāna, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*. The second chapter:
A summary verse on the excellence of going for refuge.

Indeed, he who has gone for refuge here in this vehicle should be known as the supreme refuge among all those who have gone for refuge, distinguished by fourfold aspects of meaning through the distinctions of universal presence, acceptance, realization, and mastery. (MSA 2.1)
Because this resolve is difficult at the outset and hard to accomplish even in many thousands of aeons;
and because, once perfected, it achieves the great purpose of establishing the welfare of sentient beings—therefore, the vehicle is supreme here for the sake of being the foremost refuge.

He who is committed to ferrying across all sentient beings, who is endowed with skill in the knowledge that pervades all, and who is of one single flavor regarding both nirvāṇa and saṃsāra—he should be known as a wise one who is thus all-pervading. (MSA 2.3)
Having gone to this refuge of great purpose, he attains an immeasurable increase in the multitude of his virtues;
he vibrates throughout this world with an intention of compassion and spreads the incomparable Dharma of great value.
The second chapter on Going for Refuge in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra. The third chapter:
A summary verse on the distinctions of the spiritual lineage (gotra).
The preeminence among beings, its intrinsic nature, its signs, the distinctions of the lineage, its disadvantages, its benefits, and the two kinds of similes—these are fourfold. (MSA 3.1)

The existence of the spiritual lineage (gotra) is established through the distinctions among the elements (dhātu), inclinations (adhimukti), and practices (pratipatti), as well as through the observation of differences in their results.
Because it is the cause of excellence, universality, great purpose, and inexhaustibility regarding the wholesome, the preeminence of the lineage (gotra) is established.
Naturally perfected, it consists of both the basis and that which is based upon it;
it should be understood as both existent and non-existent, in the sense of being the means for crossing over the qualities.

Compassion, resolute faith, patience, and excellent conduct from the very beginning of practice— these are determined to be the signs of the spiritual lineage (gotra), even for one who is currently virtuous.
The lineage is determinate or indeterminate, and it is either unshakable or indeed shakable;
this classification of lineages is, in brief, fourfold according to its conditions.

The disadvantages of the spiritual lineage (gotra) should be known, in brief, as being fourfold: the habituation to afflictions, association with bad friends, misfortune, and dependence on others. (MSA 3.7)
After a long time, there is departure for the miserable realms, yet swift liberation from them; there, one experiences only slight suffering with a sense of urgency, thereby maturing sentient beings.
It should be known as being like a gold mine, the locus of immeasurable purity,
and the basis for the powers of the conjunction with the stainlessness of primordial wisdom.

It should be known as being like a precious jewel-lineage, because it is the cause of great enlightenment, and because it is the basis for great wisdom, noble meditative concentration, and the welfare of great beings. (MSA 3.10)
Some are exclusively devoted to misconduct; some have eradicated their wholesome qualities;
some possess no merit conducive to liberation; and some have inferior wholesomeness or are even devoid of the cause.

When the profound and sublime teaching, proclaimed for the sake of benefiting others, is presented as the Dharma of long duration, those who possess the nature and qualities of a bodhisattva develop an exceedingly vast conviction toward it even without understanding it, and they are capable of its actual practice. That they attain, at the conclusion, the supreme fulfillment pertaining to both [self and others] should be known as resulting from their lineage being nourished by that very [Dharma]. (MSA 3.12)

Because it results in the growth of the tree of awakening with its vast qualities, and in the attainment of wealth, happiness, and the pacification of suffering, this noble lineage (gotra) is preeminent, as it brings about the performance of deeds for the benefit and happiness of both oneself and others. (MSA 3.13)
The third chapter on the lineage in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*. The fourth chapter:
A verse concerning the characteristics of the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).

The volition of Bodhisattvas—great in its enthusiasm, great in its undertaking, for the sake of the great goal, and resulting in great success—is the source of the mind, possessing a twofold purpose. (MSA 4.1)

The production of the thought of enlightenment is considered to be: that which consists of resolute conviction, another which consists of pure high resolve, that which is maturational throughout the stages, and likewise that which is free from obstructions.
This [great compassion] is held to have compassion as its root, a constant intention for the welfare of sentient beings,
resolute confidence in the Dharma, and likewise, an objective support consisting of the search for knowledge of that [Dharma].
He who is driven by superior aspiration has the restraint of ethical discipline as his foundation;
his exertion consists in the removal of opposing factors, and his endurance in the overcoming of obstacles. (MSA 4.4)
For that [path] consists of merit and wisdom, and it possesses the benefit of the increase of virtue;
it is described as always having the perfections (pāramitās) as its yoga and its departure (niryāṇa).
This determination regarding the production of the thought of enlightenment by Bodhisattvas should be understood as culminating in the [ten] stages, each according to its own specific application.

The arising of the thought of enlightenment is said to have an unstable or stable emergence, depending on the power of a friend, the power of the cause, the power of the root, the power of hearing, the practice of virtue, or the instruction of another. (MSA 4.7)
For one who has well-served the Perfectly Awakened One and has thoroughly accumulated the equipment of wisdom and merit,
there is the supremacy of this [path] due to the arising of non-conceptual knowledge regarding all phenomena.
Because he attains a mind of equanimity toward phenomena, sentient beings, their welfare, and supreme Buddhahood, his joy is distinguished by its excellence.

Nobility of birth, enthusiasm for that [path], purity of intention, skill in the remaining [perfections], and indeed the final departure (niryāṇa) are to be understood [as the characteristics]. (MSA 4.10)
Born from the seed of resolute faith in the Dharma and from the supreme mother of the perfections,
he grows within the blissful womb consisting of meditative concentration, with compassion as his nurturing nurse.
Magnanimity is to be understood from the accomplishment of the ten great vows;
enthusiasm is to be recognized through tirelessness despite hardships and long durations. (MSA 4.12)

The purity of intention should be understood as arising from the realization of near-enlightenment and from the attainment of the knowledge of its means; skillfulness, however, pertains to the other stages.

Departure is to be understood through mental attention according to its established arrangement, through the knowledge that it is a conceptual construction, and through non-conceptualization of that very [construction]. (MSA 4.14)
The arising [of the lineage] is to be known as equal to the earth; another is like fine gold; it resembles the new white moon; and another exalted [lineage] is like fire. (MSA 4.15)
Furthermore, one [type of bodhisattva] is like a great treasure-store, another is like a mine of jewels;
one should know that [others] are like the ocean, like a diamond, and like the immovable king of mountains.
Another should be known as resembling the King of Medicine (Bhaiṣajyarāja) and like a great friend;
another should be known as shining like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) and similar to the sun.
One is to be known as being like the sweet voice of a gandharva; another is comparable to a king; another resembles a storehouse; and likewise, another is like a great highway. (MSA 4.18)
It should be understood as being like a vehicle, like a gandharva-city, and like the source of a reed-thicket;
it is similar to the sound of joy and like the current of a great river. (MSA 4.19)
The production of the thought of enlightenment by the sons of the Conquerors is indeed described as being like a cloud;
therefore, with joyful hearts, one should produce that mind which is so rich in virtues.

Because they have attained the mind directed toward the welfare of others, because they have found the means thereto, and because they perceive the true meaning of the great intentional teachings, those people who lack the arising of such a noble mind will go to a mere quiescence, abandoning that [supreme] bliss.
Simultaneously with the arising of the excellent mind of the wise one, the mind is well-restrained from infinite misdeeds;
being virtuous and compassionate, he always rejoices in both pleasure and pain, increasing these two.
When one disregards even one's own body and life to undergo supreme exertion for the sake of others,
how could such a person ever engage in an evil deed that involves harming others?
Having perceived all phenomena as being like an illusion and rebirths as being like a journey,
he does not fear either afflictions or suffering, whether in times of prosperity or in times of adversity.

For those whose nature is eternal compassion, their own virtues, the joy arising from the welfare of sentient beings, intentional rebirth, and the miraculous transformations of supernatural power are their ornaments, their food, their supreme ground, and their delight in play. (MSA 4.25)

For one who is devoted to the welfare of others and possesses a compassionate nature, even the Avīci hell becomes a place of delight; how much less, then, would such a person fear existence (saṃsāra), which arises from the suffering dependent upon others? (MSA 4.26)

For one whose self is constantly permeated by the teacher of great compassion, whose mind is tormented by the sufferings of others, there arises extreme shame when others must again urge them on toward the welfare of others whenever such a task has arisen. (MSA 4.27)
The Supreme Being, who has placed the heavy burden of sentient beings upon his head, does not look graceful with faltering steps;
being bound by the various fetters of self and others, he ought to exert himself a hundredfold.
In the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, the fourth chapter on the Generation of the Thought [of Enlightenment] is concluded;
here begins the fifth chapter, the chapter on the Characteristics of Practice, with its first verse.
The practice of the sons of the Conquerors is held to consist in a great basis, a great undertaking, and the arising of great fruit;
it always effects the great gift, the great endurance, and the performance of the task of accomplishing the great purpose. (MSA 5.1)

Having attained a mind of equality toward others, or even regarding others as more dear than oneself, one who thus perceives the welfare of others as superior to one's own—what is one's own interest, and what is the interest of others? (MSA 5.2)

In the world beyond, no enemy proceeds with such mercilessness toward his foe through acts of torment as one whose nature is compassion proceeds toward himself for the sake of others, undergoing intense suffering and torment.
For those established in inferior, middling, or superior natures, there is well-taught instruction, attraction, and introduction;
training in the meaning, ripening in the wholesome, as well as advice, stability, intelligence, and liberation. (MSA 5.4)

The attainment through distinguished qualities, the arising of the lineage, the prophecy and consecration, the knowledge of a Tathāgata, and the unsurpassed state—this is the welfare of others, consisting of thirteen [stages]. (MSA 5.5)
Teaching that conforms to people and is non-erroneous, free from pride, without "mine-ness," and discerning;
patient, self-controlled, far-reaching, and inexhaustible—this is the supreme practice of the sons of the Victors. (MSA 5.6)

In great fear, those who crave sensual desires proceed; those who love existence proceed in unstable, inverted pleasure; those who love peace proceed toward the pacification of their own individual suffering; but those whose nature is compassion always proceed toward the pacification of all suffering.
The deluded person, ever striving for their own happiness, fails to attain it and instead falls into suffering;
the wise person, however, always striving for the sake of others, accomplishes the welfare of both and attains final peace.
In whatever way the Son of the Conqueror, engaged in his course of conduct, proceeds within the diverse range of sensory objects,
in that very way he applies himself to the welfare of sentient beings through words of appropriate and equalizing meaning.

A wise person does not harbor resentment toward those whose minds are rendered powerless by their faults; for he recognizes that such transgressions occur against one's will, and thus his compassion increases. (MSA 5.10)
Practice itself is that which transcends all states of existence, follows supreme peace,
increases through various multitudes of virtues, and always embraces the world with a compassionate intention. (MSA 5.11)
In the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, the fifth chapter on Practice is concluded;
now follows the verse concerning the sixth chapter, the Analysis of the Characteristics of the Ultimate Truth.
Neither existent nor non-existent, neither thus nor otherwise; it is not born, it does not perish, it does not diminish;
it does not increase, nor is it purified, yet it is purified again—this is the characteristic of the ultimate reality (paramārtha).
The view of self is not itself characterized by a self, nor is its state of being ill-established (duḥsaṃsthitatā) something distinct from it;
it is nothing other than these two. This delusion has arisen from them, and therefore liberation is simply the exhaustion of that delusion.

How is it that people, relying on mere delusion, do not realize the continuous nature of suffering? [The person] is neither a knower nor a non-knower, neither afflicted nor unafflicted, consisting of dharmas yet not consisting of them. (MSA 6.3)
How is it that people, whose activity is directed toward what is directly perceived, rely on [the notion of] being produced by another when things arise through dependent origination?
What kind of darkness is this, such that, failing to see [reality], they perceive both existence and non-existence? (MSA 6.4)
In this world, from the perspective of the ultimate reality, there is no distinction whatsoever between these two: tranquility and birth.
Nevertheless, for those who perform virtuous deeds, the attainment of tranquility is established through the cessation of birth.
Having accumulated the infinite and boundless equipment of wisdom and merit, the bodhisattva,
through the thorough ascertainment of reflection regarding all phenomena, arrives at the realization that the nature of objects follows from mental discourse.
Having realized that objects are mere verbal designations, he abides in the state of mind-only which appears as those [objects];
thus the dharmadhātu becomes directly manifest to him, and he is thereby liberated from the characteristic of duality.
Having realized through the intellect that there is nothing other than mind, one arrives at the non-existence of the mind itself;
therefore, having realized the non-existence of both, the wise person abides in the realm of phenomena which is free from those two.

By the power of non-conceptual knowledge, which is always and universally accompanied by wisdom, the accumulation of faults that is as deep as a cavern—residing in that [knowledge]—is cast out, just as poison is removed by a great medicine. (MSA 6.9)

Firmly established in the excellent Dharma ordained by the Sage, having fixed his mind upon the dharmadhātu along with its root, and having understood that the course of mindfulness is merely a mental construction, the steadfast one swiftly goes to the further shore of the ocean of qualities.
In the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, the sixth chapter is the Chapter on Reality;
the seventh chapter is the Analysis of the Characteristics of Power, beginning with this verse:

The speech regarding arising, the mind, the auspicious and inauspicious, their bases, and the state of essencelessness—this knowledge, which is unimpeded regarding all things in their various divisions even when beyond the senses, is the power belonging to the steadfast one. (MSA 7.1)
Having attained the perfectly pure fourth dhyāna through the embrace of non-conceptual knowledge,
one reaches supreme accomplishment of power by means of mental attention according to the established order.
By means of which he constantly dwells in noble, divine, and incomparable abodes, as well as in sublime Brahmā-like states;
and having gone to the various directions, he honors the Buddhas and brings sentient beings to purity.
He perceives all world-systems, together with their sentient beings and their processes of evolution and dissolution, as being like an illusion;
and having attained mastery, he manifests them exactly as he desires, even in their various diverse forms.
By the emission of light rays, he causes those in the miserable realms who are intensely suffering to go to heaven;
and by shaking the splendor of the palaces belonging to the lineage of Māra, he terrifies them along with their Māras.
He displays immeasurable mastery over meditative concentration in the midst of the foremost assembly;
and through his karma, births, and supreme emanations, he constantly attends to the welfare of sentient beings at all times.
Through mastery over knowledge, he attains the purification of his field for the purpose of manifesting it according to his will;
and by proclaiming the name of the Buddha in worlds where there is no name of a Buddha, he transfers those beings to another realm.
And he indeed becomes capable of ripening sentient beings, just like a bird whose wings have grown;
he receives excessive praise from the Buddha and his speech becomes authoritative for all people.
The sixfold supernormal knowledges, the three types of clear knowledge, the eight liberations, and likewise the eight bases of mastery;
the ten totalities as well, and the immeasurable concentrations—this is the power belonging to the wise.
For he, having attained the intellect of supreme mastery, constantly brings the world—which is otherwise powerless—under his own control;
delighting solely in performing the welfare of others, the wise one moves through the realms of existence as steadfastly as a lion.
The seventh chapter on Power in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The eighth chapter: A summary verse on the maturation of the bodhisattva.

Zeal, clarity, tranquility, compassion, patience, as well as intelligence and strength, and being fully endowed with the limbs that cannot be shaken—this, O Son of the Conqueror, is the characteristic of its maturation. (MSA 8.1)

The triad beginning with friendliness, formidable heroism, and the gathering of the supreme dharma that culminates in the ultimate good—this is considered the characteristic of perfect maturation for a compassionate one in the great undertaking of the true dharma. (MSA 8.2)

Knowing the qualities [of the Teacher], the swift attainment of meditative concentration, the experience of the fruit, and the non-differentiation of the mind—these are considered the characteristics of perfect maturation for the sake of full realization toward the Son of the Victor, the Teacher. (MSA 8.3)

Perfect restraint, the avoidance of afflicted discursive thoughts, the absence of obstacles, and delight in the virtuous—these are considered the bases for dispelling afflictions in a Son of the Victor; indeed, they are the characteristics of correct maturation. (MSA 8.4)

Compassion by nature, the perception of the suffering of others, the complete abandonment of a base mind, the attainment of distinction, and being born as the foremost in the world—these are the characteristics of the maturation of supreme empathy for others. (MSA 8.5)

Fortitude by nature, the cultivation of analytical discernment, the constant endurance of intense suffering, cold, and so forth, the tendency toward excellence, and delight in the virtuous— this is considered the characteristic of the maturation of patience.

Purity of maturation consists in not forgetting upon hearing and so forth, as well as penetrating what is well-spoken and ill-spoken; furthermore, it is the fitness for the arising of great intelligence and the characteristic of the full ripening of excellent wisdom.
Through the two types of merit, there is the nourishment of the two realms; at the arising of the fruit, there is supreme fitness of the basis.
The attainment of one's heart's desire and the state of being the foremost in the world—these are the characteristics of maturation upon the acquisition of power.

The characteristic of the maturation of being unshakable is: an intention that investigates through reasoning according to the true nature of reality, the attainment of excellence, the refutation of opposing positions, and furthermore, the constant absence of obstacles from Māra.
The accumulation of merit, the fitness of the basis for effort, and the delight in sublime seclusion—
these, O Son of the Conqueror, are considered the characteristics of the perfect maturation when the factors [of enlightenment] are fully endowed.

Thus, with his self matured by the ninefold subject matter and having attained the fitness to mature others, his self constantly increased by the nature of pure [dharmas], he always becomes the supreme kinsman of the world. (MSA 8.11)
Just as ripening is desired for both a wound and food, so that they may become fit for draining and consumption respectively;
likewise, in this basis (the āśraya), there is the pacification of the two sides, and the state of being fit for enjoyment through the well-pacified side.
For embodied beings, there is said to be ripening (*vipācana*), as well as full ripening (*paripācanā*), further ripening (*prapācanā*), and another called subsequent ripening (*anupācanā*);
furthermore, excellent ripening (*supācanā*), superior ripening (*adhipācanā*), downward ripening (*nipācanā*), and upward ripening (*utpācanā*) are recognized.
Just as a son of the Conqueror remains here established with a heart of benefit, maturing the entire world,
neither mother, nor father, nor kinsmen are so well-established toward their children or their relatives.

Likewise, ordinary people are not considered to be as affectionate toward themselves as a compassionate being is toward other sentient beings who are very dear to them; for the latter seeks to establish them in welfare and happiness as if they were their own self. (MSA 8.15)
There is nothing whatsoever that a bodhisattva cannot give away to others from their own body or possessions;
maturing others through these two kinds of assistance, they are never satiated by the qualities of giving equally.
Always by nature supremely non-violent, himself delighting in this [virtue] and being heedful, he establishes others in it;
performing benefit for others in two ways, he ripens them through the qualities of both maturation and natural outflow.
Regarding those who cause harm, one who possesses the perception of them as benefactors endures even their severe transgressions;
through skillful means and a mind intent on enduring injuries, he leads those wrongdoers toward virtue.
Furthermore, relying upon supreme effort, that son of the Conqueror does not grow weary even throughout thousands of millions of eons,
as he brings the multitude of sentient beings to maturity for the sake of a single virtuous thought of another.
Having attained supreme mastery over the mind, he wins over others to this teaching;
having utterly destroyed all desire for honor, he causes them to increase further through virtue.
Well-ascertained in the method of the meaning of reality, he thoroughly dispels the doubts of sentient beings;
consequently, through their reverence for that teaching of the Victor, they cause themselves and others to flourish with auspicious virtues.
Thus, out of compassion, that bodhisattva leads the entire world toward a happy rebirth or toward the three types of merit by means of mild, supreme,
and intermediate methods, through a course of existence identical to that of the world.
In the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra, the eighth chapter is the Chapter on Maturation.
The ninth chapter, concerning omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), consists of two verses.
The third [verse] is an exposition of those two:

"Through hundreds of immeasurable difficult deeds, through immeasurable accumulations of merit, over an immeasurable period of time, and through the destruction of immeasurable obscurations. (MSA 9.1)
The attainment of omniscience, purified of all obscurations, is declared to be Buddhahood, like an opened casket of jewels. (MSA 9.2)

Having performed a marvelous and difficult task through hundreds of labors, having accumulated all that is auspicious over a vast period of time— the supreme vehicle of the eon— and through the exhaustion of all obscurations by uprooting even the subtle veil residing within the stages, Buddhahood is like a casket of jewels of great power that has been opened.
All phenomena are Buddhahood, yet there is no phenomenon whatsoever;
it consists of pure qualities, yet it cannot be defined by them.
Because it is the cause for the jewel of the Dharma, it is considered to have attained the likeness of a mine of jewels;
because it is the cause for the beautiful, it is considered to have attained the likeness of a cloud.

Buddhahood is both the convergence of all phenomena and yet devoid of all phenomena; it is like a vast and great mine of the jewels of Dharma because it gives rise to the extensive and great jewels of Dharma.

It is like a cloud for living beings because it is the cause for the production of the great white harvest of virtue, and because through its giving, it provides an inexhaustible, well-ordered, and extensive rain of the water of Dharma upon all creatures. (MSA 9.6)
For Buddhahood is indeed a constant protection from the entire host of afflictions,
from all misdeeds, and even from birth and death.
Therefore, it is the supreme refuge from all calamities, from the miserable realms, from lack of means, from the view of a self-identity, and from the inferior vehicle. (MSA 9.8)
That incomparable refuge is desired as the supreme state of Buddhahood; it is protection against birth, death, all afflictions, and evils.
It is the vehicle of universal protection for those fallen into various fears, and for those who have entered the lower realms of extensive and manifold suffering.

That which has a body perfectly complete with the Buddha-qualities, which knows how to discipline sentient beings through the true Dharma, and which has reached the further shore out of compassion for all worlds—that is Buddhahood, the most excellent refuge here in this world. (MSA 9.10)
From the beginning of time, Buddhahood has been the great refuge for all sentient beings;
it is considered the means for the reversal of all calamities and the attainment of prosperity. (MSA 9.11)

When the seed of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable, which has persisted for an exceedingly long time, comes to an end through all the vast modes of abandonment, there occurs Buddhahood—the transformation of the basis endowed with the most excellent qualities of pure dharmas; its attainment is through the path of non-conceptual knowledge, which is utterly purified and has the Great Object as its domain. (MSA 9.12)
Established therein, that Tathāgata gazes upon the world as if standing atop a great mountain-king;
he takes compassion for people who delight in tranquility, so what need is there to mention those other people who delight in evil and existence? (MSA 9.13)

The transformation of the Tathāgatas is held to be characterized by activity and non-activity, by basis, by cessation and non-cessation, as well as by duality and non-duality; it is both equal and distinguished, and has the nature of being all-pervading.
Just as space is always all-pervading and unconditioned, so too is that [Buddha-nature] always all-pervading and unconditioned;
just as space is omnipresent among the multitudes of forms, so too is it omnipresent among the multitudes of sentient beings.
Just as the reflection of the moon is not seen when a water vessel is broken,
so too the form of the Buddha is not seen among corrupt sentient beings.
Just as a fire blazes in one place and then subsides in another,
so too should the appearance and disappearance of the Buddhas be understood.
Just as the production of sound occurs from musical instruments that have not been struck,
so too does the emergence of the teaching arise from the Jina even without deliberate effort.
Just as a jewel displays its own radiance without effort,
so too do the Buddhas manifest their activities without exertion.
Just as worldly activities are seen to proceed without interruption in space,
so too do the deeds of the Victors proceed without interruption in the untainted realm.
Just as in space there is always the cessation and the arising of activities,
so too in the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu) there is the arising and passing away of the Buddha's work.
Although it is undifferentiated by priority or posteriority, and free from all obscurations,
suchness is considered to be Buddhahood— neither pure nor impure.
When emptiness is purified through the attainment of the path of selflessness,
the Buddhas, by virtue of attaining the pure self, have reached the state of the Great Self.
Buddhahood is said to be neither existence nor non-existence;
therefore, regarding the question of the nature of the Buddha, the method of the undeclared (avyākṛta) is held to be appropriate.
Just as the cessation of heat occurs in iron and the disappearance of cataracts occurs in vision,
so too in the Buddha’s knowledge of the mind, neither existence nor non-existence is praised.
In the stainless realm of the Buddhas, there is neither unity nor plurality;
because they are bodiless like space, yet [appear] in accordance with their previous bodies.
Enlightenment is considered to be like a mine of jewels with respect to the Buddha-qualities such as power, and like a great cloud with respect to the crops of virtue in the world. (MSA 9.27)
Because it is completely filled with merit and wisdom, it is considered like the full moon;
and because it produces the light of knowledge, it is considered like the great sun.
Just as immeasurable rays, though intermingled within the orb of the sun, always function with a single purpose and illuminate the world; so too [are the Buddha's qualities].
In the same way, within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), the Buddhas are immeasurable;
they perform their activities with a unified purpose, bringing forth the light of wisdom.
Just as from the emission of a single ray all rays are emitted from the sun,
so too should the emission of the wisdom of the Buddhas be understood.
Just as there is no sense of "mine" in the functioning of the sun's rays,
so too there is no sense of "mine" in the functioning of the Buddhas' gnoses.
Just as the world is illuminated all at once by the rays of light emitted from the single sun,
so too is the entire object of knowledge illuminated simultaneously by the wisdoms of a Buddha.
Just as the obscuration of the sun's rays is considered to be clouds and the like, so too the obscuration of the Buddhas' gnosis is the corruption of sentient beings. (MSA 9.34)

Just as the variegation or lack of variegation in colors on a cloth depends upon the dye, so too the variegation or lack of variegation in knowledge within liberation depends upon the absence of obstruction.
The profundity of the Buddhas regarding the stainless realm, its characteristics, its stations, and its activities, has been described as being like painting the sky with colors.
Although suchness is undifferentiated for all, when it has attained purity, it is the state of a Tathāgata; therefore, all embodied beings possess that as their embryo (tadgarbha).
By the mastery of the Śrāvakas, that of worldly beings is surpassed;
by the mind belonging to the level of the Pratyekabuddhas, that of the Śrāvaka is surpassed. (MSA 9.38)
It does not approach even a fraction of the sovereign power of a bodhisattva;
it does not approach even a fraction of the sovereign power of a Tathāgata.
The sovereign power of a Buddha is held to be immeasurable and inconceivable;
it is that which operates for whomever, wherever, in whatever manner, to whatever extent, and at whatever time.
Upon the transformation of the five faculties, supreme mastery is attained in the engagement with all objects and in the arising of twelve hundred qualities for all of them. (MSA 9.41)
Upon the revolution of the mind as well, supreme mastery is attained,
in a non-conceptual and perfectly pure gnosis that accompanies that mastery.
Upon the revolution of the grasping of the object, supreme mastery is attained for the sake of purifying the field, so that enjoyments may be manifested according to one's wish.
Upon the revolution of conceptual construction, supreme mastery is attained, characterized by the perpetual absence of obstruction in all forms of knowledge and action at all times. (MSA 9.44)
Upon the revolution of the basis, supreme mastery is attained:
the non-abiding nirvana of the Buddhas in the immovable and stainless state.
Upon the transformation of sexual desire, supreme mastery is attained:
in dwelling in the bliss of a Buddha, and in perceiving one’s wife without defilement. (MSA 9.46)
Upon the reversal of the perception of space, supreme mastery is attained, as well as the fulfillment of intended aims and the manifestation of movement and form. (MSA 9.47)

Thus, when there is the revolution of the immeasurable, the sovereignty over the immeasurable is considered to belong to the Buddhas in their stainless basis, due to the performance of inconceivable activities.
When the world has increased its virtue, it proceeds toward supreme purity; and by not abandoning virtue, it proceeds toward the highest state through the increase of virtue.
Thus the world, whether immature or mature, proceeds in every direction according to the well-spoken teachings of the Victors; yet here, there is certainly no one who is entirely without remainder.

Having thus practiced the conduct that is difficult to attain, the steadfast ones obtain in every direction at all times and forever that Great Enlightenment—which is endowed with supreme qualities, wondrous in its manifestation, eternal, constant, and a refuge for those without refuge. This is a marvel in the world because of their practice of the excellent method; yet it is not a marvel [to them], as they have acted accordingly. (MSA 9.50)
In some places he displays the wheel of Dharma through hundreds of diverse gateways; in some places the disappearance of birth, and in others the various activities of beings;
in some places complete enlightenment, and in others nirvana repeatedly—yet he does not waver from that state, and yet he accomplishes everything.
It does not occur to the Buddhas, "This person has been ripened by me," or "This embodied being is not yet ripe," or even "He is being ripened right now.
Yet, without any deliberate effort, the multitude of beings indeed reaches full ripening through wholesome qualities, constantly and everywhere in every direction, through the three gates.
Just as the sun, by its widespread and pure rays of light, brings about the ripening of crops in every direction and on all sides without effort;
so too does the Sun of Dharma, by means of its spreading rays of the Dharma that consist of the methods for pacification, bring about the ripening of crops in every direction and on all sides.
Just as from a single lamp there arises a vast multitude of lamps, immeasurable and incalculable, yet that original lamp does not thereby undergo exhaustion;
so too, from a single Buddha there arises a vast multitude of ripenings, immeasurable and incalculable, yet that original ripening does not thereby undergo exhaustion. (MSA 9.54)

Just as the great ocean does not reach satiety nor undergo increase by the entry of vast quantities of clear water, so too the Buddha-element reaches neither satiety nor increase through the constant and continuous entries of purification; this is a supreme marvel here. (MSA 9.55)
It is characterized by the purity of suchness, which is free from the two obscurations regarding all phenomena;
it is characterized by the inexhaustible mastery over the knowledge of reality and its objective support.

The perfection of the purification of the suchness of all phenomena, characterized by the exhaustion of the two obscurations—those of afflictions and the knowable—and the characteristic of inexhaustible mastery over both the object and the knowledge that takes it as its object;

the attainment resulting from the cultivation of the knowledge of suchness in every respect; and the fruit, which is the inexhaustibility of providing the two [benefits] to all sentient beings in every way. (MSA 9.57)
Its activity consists of the application of the emanations of body, speech, and mind through skillful means;
it is endowed with the two gateways of meditative concentration and mnemonic formulas, as well as the two immeasurables.

This pure realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) of the Buddhas is declared to function through distinct modes as the nature-body (svabhāvakāya), the enjoyment-body (saṃbhogakāya), and the emanation-body (nirmāṇakāya). // MSA_9.59 //
The body of essential nature, the enjoyment body, and another, the transformation body—these are indeed the divisions of the bodies of the Buddhas; the first, however, is the basis for the other two.
In all realms, the Enjoyment Body is differentiated by its assemblies of followers, its fields, its names, its bodies, and its activities for the enjoyment of the Dharma. (MSA 9.61)
The natural body (svābhāvikakāya) is considered to be even, subtle, and closely joined;
it is the cause for the mastery of enjoyment in manifesting enjoyments at will.
The immeasurable emanation of the Buddha is considered the nirmāṇakāya;
in it, the fulfillment of the two purposes for both [self and others] is established in all its aspects.
Through the display of craftsmanship, birth, great enlightenment, and constant nirvana,
this emanation body of the Buddha is a great illusion (or great skillful means) for the sake of liberation.
The collection of the bodies of the Buddhas is to be understood through three bodies;
that which constitutes the welfare of oneself and others, together with its basis, is demonstrated by these three bodies.
They are considered equal in terms of their basis, their intention, and their action; their permanence is found in their nature, their non-interruption, and their continuity. (MSA 9.66)
Mirror-like wisdom is immovable; the other three wisdoms are based upon it—namely, the wisdom of equality, the wisdom of discernment, and the wisdom of accomplishing activities.
Mirror-like wisdom is free from the notion of "mine," undivided, and ever-present;
it is unconfused regarding all objects of knowledge, yet it is never directed toward them.

Because it is the cause of all-knowledge, the state of the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogabuddhatā) is like a great mine of wisdom; and because it is the source from which the reflections of wisdom arise, it is so compared.
The knowledge of equality toward sentient beings is considered stainless due to the purity of cultivation;
it is held to be the knowledge of equality that has entered into non-abiding tranquility.
And it is considered to be accompanied by great loving-kindness and compassion at all times,
manifesting the image of the Buddha to sentient beings according to their respective inclinations.
The wisdom of discernment is always unimpeded regarding all objects of knowledge,
and it is like a treasury of dhāraṇīs and samādhis.
It displays all sovereign powers within the circle of the assembly,
cuts through all doubts, and rains down the great Dharma.
The knowledge of the performance of duties, through emanations in all realms—varied, immeasurable, and inconceivable—effects the welfare of all sentient beings. (MSA 9.74)
The inconceivable emanation of the Buddha is to be understood at all times through its various types, the accomplishment of tasks, its numbers, and its fields; and it is to be known in every respect.
From retention, from equanimity of mind, from the correct illumination of the Dharma,
and from the performance of duties, there arises the fourfold gnosis.

Because of the distinction of lineages, because of non-futility, because of completeness, and also because of beginninglessness; and because there is no difference [in nature], there is neither a single Buddhahood nor multiplicity in the stainless locus. (MSA 9.77)
That which is non-existence is itself the supreme existence;
and non-apprehension in every respect is considered the supreme apprehension.
For those who do not perceive cultivation, cultivation is considered supreme;
for those who perceive cultivation, attainment is considered supreme.
For those conceited bodhisattvas who perceive that [perfection] as a heavy burden, as something distant, and as a long-term cause requiring their own effort, awakening is said to be far away.
For those who perceive that all this as it has been described is mere conceptual construction,
enlightenment is said to be attained by Bodhisattvas who are free from conceptualization.

Rivers whose bases are separate and whose waters are distinct have little water; they perform diverse functions and are enjoyed only by the small creatures that depend on their water, as they have not entered the depths of the underworld.
And once they have entered the ocean, they all become based on a single foundation and constitute one great body of water;
unified in their activity, they are always a source of great enjoyment for the multitude of beings that depend upon the waters.

Those who have not entered into Buddhahood have distinct bases and differing views; being wise yet possessing only slight awakening, they perform their duties individually and are always available for the benefit of limited beings. (MSA 9.84)
And having entered into Buddhahood, they all share a single basis and a single great awakening;
their activities are unified and they are always a source of great enjoyment for the multitude of great beings.
Thus, because of its union with incomparable pure qualities, because it is the cause of benefit and happiness for the stage of Buddhahood,
and because it is a mine of supreme, inexhaustible, and auspicious bliss, one of virtuous mind deserves to attain the thought of enlightenment.
The ninth chapter on Enlightenment in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra. The tenth chapter: Summary Verse.
The beginning, accomplishment, refuge, lineage, and likewise the production of the thought [of awakening];
the welfare of oneself and others, the meaning of reality, spiritual power, maturation, and enlightenment. (MSA 10.1)
Arising again and again, it is that which grasps, that which is grasped, received from a friend, derived from oneself, and erroneous;
another is non-erroneous; another is manifest, while yet another is neither; it is that which functions through sound, that which seeks, and that which examines. (MSA 10.2)
Resolute belief (adhimukti) may be removable or unremovable by opposing factors; inferior or sublime; obscured or unobscured;
associated or dissociated; accumulated or unaccumulated; deeply entered, or far-reaching. (MSA 10.3)
An abundance of improper mental attention, laziness, error regarding yoga, bad friends, weakness in virtue, and irrational mental attention. (MSA 10.4)
Heedlessness, limited learning, contentment with little study or reflection, pride in mere tranquility, and likewise a lack of mastery are considered [the obstacles]. (MSA 10.5)
Lack of agitation, as well as agitation, obscuration, lack of application,
and lack of accumulation are to be known as obstacles to resolute belief.
Great merit, freedom from regret, great mental joy, and happiness;
non-wastage, stability, and likewise the attainment of distinction. (MSA 10.7)
The clear realization of the Dharma, the attainment of the supreme welfare of oneself and others,
and the possession of swift super-knowledge— these indeed are the benefits arising from resolute belief.
To those possessed by desire, it is like a dog; to those in meditative concentration, it resembles a tortoise;
to those seeking their own welfare, it is comparable to a servant; and to those seeking the welfare of others, it is like a king. (MSA 10.9)

Likewise, one should always recognize the distinction in those who have arisen for the sake of their own desires, for abiding [in the vehicle], and for performing the duties for themselves and others, through their various forms of resolute belief (*adhimukti*) in the Mahāyāna. Having understood its supreme nature here according to the rule, the steadfast person should always and intensely choose only those [resolutions] in this world.
Since immeasurable beings who have become human attain perfect enlightenment at every moment, one should therefore not succumb to despondency.
Just as one who gives food to others generates merit, but not so the great arising of merit for one who eats it himself. (MSA 10.12)
That which is taught in the Sūtras is obtained from the Dharma taught for the sake of others;
it is not, however, obtained from the Dharma taught for one's own sake.
Thus, having generated a mind of great resolve for the vast and noble Dharma that flows like a great flood, the wise one, possessing great faith,
proceeds toward vast and constant merit, its further increase, and through incomparable qualities, toward the state of a Great Being.
In the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, the tenth chapter is the Chapter on Devotion;
the eleventh chapter is the Chapter on the Search for the Dharma. Within the search for the object [of meditation], there are four verses.
The three baskets, or alternatively two,
are intended by way of nine reasons through their summary;
they liberate by means of impregnation, awakening, pacification, and penetration.
In brief, the Sūtra, Abhidharma, and Vinaya are considered to have four types of meaning;
through the knowledge of these, the wise one attains omniscience in all its aspects.
The Sūtra is so called because it indicates [the teaching] by way of its basis, its characteristics, its phenomena, and its meaning;
and the Abhidharma is so called because it is directed toward [the truth], because it is repeated, and because it surpasses and reaches [the goal]. (MSA 11.3)
The nature of discipline (*vinaya*) consists of: the offense, its origination, the emergence from it, and the departure from it;
as well as [its establishment] through the person, its formal designation, its classification, and its definitive determination. (MSA 11.4)
The object of focus is considered to be the dharmas, both internal and external;
the attainment of the two is by means of the two meanings, and through the non-apprehension of the two.

Through mental verbalizations, through the sustained concentration of one who has faith in the meaning as it has been explained, through the appearance of the object from verbalization, and through the mind's abiding in the name. (MSA 11.6)
The attainment of the object that is the Dharma occurs through the three types of knowledge, beginning with that derived from hearing;
and the previously mentioned threefold attainment of objects is based upon that.
One [type of aspiration] pertains to the three realms; another performs what is to be done; another has a basis that involves constraint;
and another is characterized by the settling of resolute belief and produces intense zeal.

The basis is twofold, being either deficient or complete; it consists of both discursive speech and non-discursiveness, and it is associated with gnosis, having the nature of the secret essence of yoga.
This [meditative concentration] has both a combined object and a distinct object;
its thorough knowledge is fivefold and sevenfold, and its [resulting] mastery is fivefold.
The thirty-seven aspects are comprised within cultivation;
this [path] has the two paths as its intrinsic nature, possesses two benefits, and is receptive.
The preparatory, the sovereign, the limited, and that which consists of the vast—
this mental engagement of yogins is considered to be of every kind.

Reality is that which is eternally devoid of duality, the basis of error, and absolutely incapable of being expressed; it is of a non-conceptual nature, to be known, abandoned, and purified, and is considered by nature to be stainless, its purification from afflictions being regarded as similar to that of space, gold, and water. (MSA 11.13)
Indeed, there exists nothing else in the world apart from that [reality], yet the entire world has its intellect utterly deluded regarding it.
How has this form of worldly delusion arisen, such that one is attached to what is non-existent while completely abandoning what is real? (MSA 11.14)
Just as an illusion is described, so is unreal imagination;
just as that which is produced by illusion, so is the delusion of duality described.
Just as the non-existence of that [object] therein is accepted as ultimate reality (paramārtha),
so too its perception is accepted as conventional reality (saṃvṛtisatya).
Just as manifestation of the cause of that [manifestation] is obtained when it is absent,
so too, upon the revolution of the basis, the manifestation of that which is like a non-existent is obtained.
Just as the world, being undeluded regarding those signs, may act according to its desire, so too the Lord (or ascetic), having undergone transformation, acts at will, free from error.
Its form exists there, yet its substantial reality is not found;
therefore, both existence and non-existence are predicated of illusions and the like.
Therein, existence is not non-existence, nor is non-existence simply existence;
rather, the non-distinction between existence and non-existence is established in the case of illusions and the like.
Thus, the appearance of duality exists there, yet its actual existence is not found;
therefore, both existence and non-existence are predicated of form and the other aggregates.
Therein, existence is not non-existence, and non-existence is indeed not existence;
moreover, the non-distinction between existence and non-existence is established in respect to form and the other [sense objects].
It is intended for the purpose of negating the extremes of superimposition and denial,
and specifically for the purpose of negating the departure by means of the Hīnayāna.

The cause of error and the error itself are held to be the representation of form and the representation that is formless; for if the latter did not exist, the former could not exist due to its non-existence.
The duality is illustrated by the error of grasping at the form of an illusory elephant;
therein, the duality does not exist in the way it appears, yet the duality is nevertheless perceived.
The duality is taught due to the delusion of grasping at the reflection and the skeleton;
therein, the duality does not exist in the way it appears, yet duality is indeed perceived.
Because they exist in such a way and do not exist in such a way, and because there is no distinction between existence and non-existence,
those phenomena characterized by delusion are both existent and non-existent, like illusory things.
Because they do not exist in such a way, because they do not exist in such a way, and because they do not exist in such a way,
those remedial factors which are taught as being like an illusion are without defining characteristics.
Like a king of illusion defeated by another king of illusion,
those sons of the Victor who perceive all phenomena as such are free from the Māra.

Like an illusion, a dream, a mirage, or a reflection; like a flash of lightning, an echo, or a bubble; like the moon’s reflection in water, and again like a magical creation—thus have the Buddhas, the supreme awakened ones, taught that the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāras) are to be understood in various contexts as six, six, two, six, two, and three respectively. MSA 11.30.
Unreal imagination is neither real nor unreal, and it is indeed non-conceptual; it is neither conceptual nor non-conceptual—all that is to be known is thus described.

From their own constituent elements, conceptual constructions arise as manifestations of duality; they are devoid of the substance of duality, yet they proceed with the activity of ignorance and the afflictions.
The attainment of the distinction of the object occurs through the application of abiding in one's own realm;
for those very [cognitions] proceed as non-dual appearances, like a hide or an arrow.
The mind is held to appear as a duality, appearing as passion and so forth; likewise, it appears as faith and so forth. There is no other distinct phenomenon that is either afflicted or wholesome.
Just as that which appears as duality is not other than the characteristic of duality, so the mind proceeds with manifold appearances and manifold forms. (MSA 11.35)

The object of definition, the definition itself, and the figurative indication—these have been fully revealed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones through their various classifications for the sake of favoring sentient beings. (MSA 11.36)

Furthermore, that mind which is accompanied by views—the state of being unchanging therein—is the object of definition (lakṣya) in brief; for it is immeasurable in its detailed classifications. (MSA 11.37)
The sign of the conceptualization of an object according to its verbal expression, the latent predisposition for that [conceptualization],
and the manifestation of the object from that [predisposition]— this is the imagined characteristic (parikalpitalakṣaṇa).
Just as there is the name, the object, and the manifestation of the object through the name— these,
being non-existent yet appearing through conceptualization, are indeed the characteristic of the imagined (parikalpita-lakṣaṇa).
The imagination of the unreal, which appears in a threefold and threefold manner and is characterized by the grasped and the grasper, is indeed the defining characteristic of the dependent nature.
The state of being both non-existence and existence, the equality of existence and non-existence,
being unpeaceful yet peaceful, and being free from conceptual construction— this is the characteristic of the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa).

Taking the outflowing dharma as the object, there is appropriate mental attention, the abiding of the mind in the realm [of reality], and the vision of the existence and non-existence of objects. (MSA 11.42)

For the noble lineage (āryagotra) is stainless; its arrival at equality therein is considered to have the characteristic of being equal, distinguished, and neither deficient nor excessive. (MSA 11.43)
The transformation of the appearance of objects and the body is the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*), resulting from the transformation of the seeds; and it is the universal basis.

There are four kinds of mastery: over the activity of the mind, over grasping, over conceptualization, and over non-conceptualization; [mastery] over the field, over knowledge, and over action. (MSA 11.45)
And on the three stages beginning with the Immovable (Acalā), that mastery is fourfold;
it is considered that there is one twofold mastery in one stage, and one mastery each in the others.
Having understood the two kinds of selflessness present here in existence, and having known them to be equal, the wise one enters reality by way of apprehension.
Then, from the stabilization of the mind therein, even that [reality] does not appear; this non-appearance is liberation, the supreme cessation of objective apprehension.
When the basis exists through the accumulation of provisions, one indeed sees that it is name-only;
seeing that it is name-only, one no longer sees even that.
This mind, always characterized by corruption and bound by the fetter of the view of self, continues to function; however, its cessation is held to result from abiding within the internal.
Because it does not exist by itself or through its own self, because its intrinsic nature is not established,
and because it is non-existent in the manner that it is grasped, it is held to be devoid of intrinsic nature.
Established by way of being without intrinsic nature, they are based one upon the next:
non-arising, non-cessation, primordial peace, and final nirvana.

Receptivity regarding the non-arising of phenomena is taught in relation to: first, identity and otherness; intrinsic characteristic; itself and its being otherwise; affliction; and finally, distinction. (MSA 11.52)

Because of the equality of the selflessness of phenomena and liberation, because of the distinction of lineages, because of the attainment of two intentions, because of emanations, and because of the ultimate limit, there is the single vehicle (ekayānatā).

The Perfectly Awakened Ones have taught the single vehicle (ekayāna) for the sake of attracting some, for the sake of maintaining others, and indeed for those who are indefinite [in their lineage]. (MSA 11.54)

The śrāvaka who is not fixed is twofold, according to whether he has seen or not seen the goal and according to his vehicle; that one who has seen the goal is both free from passion and not free from passion, and he is also weak.
And because they dedicate the noble path they have attained toward future existences,
they are endowed with an inconceivable transformative rebirth.
By the power of their vows, one attains rebirth,
while the other, through the yoga of non-returning, proceeds by means of emanations.
And because they delight in nirvāṇa, those two are considered to be of slow progress,
due to their repeated association with the active manifestation of their own minds.
Having failed to achieve his goal while born during a period without a Buddha, he exerts himself for the sake of meditative concentration;
seeking emanations, and relying upon them, he attains supreme enlightenment.

"Without applying himself to the five fields of knowledge, the supreme noble one can never attain omniscience. Thus, for the sake of refuting others, for the sake of assisting them, or for the sake of his own realization, he indeed applies himself to those fields. (MSA 11.60)
Contentment with the attainment of the cause, mindfulness of that reliance, the desire for a common fruit, and resolute conviction according to one's awakening. (MSA 11.61)
Delighting through fourfold power, the determination to overcome weariness, and the fourfold practice regarding the discordant factors and their antidotes. (MSA 11.62)
Serene confidence, patient endurance, the desire to give in future lives,
donning the armor, the vow, and the mental engagement of rejoicing.

Constant eagerness for the attainment of power; the sixfold exertion in giving and so forth; then, compassion toward those who have reached maturity, toward those who perform worship, and toward those who practice service. (MSA 11.64)
Shame regarding what is undone and what is poorly done, remorse, delight in the [spiritual] objects,
the perception of [suffering] as an enemy, and the mind that composes and elucidates [the teachings] even in the face of weariness.
Generosity and the other perfections are the refuge for awakening, not Īśvara and the like;
for one experiences both faults and virtues through these two.
Delight in recollecting [past] accumulations, seeing the great purpose, longing for yoga in the non-conceptual, and [longing] for its maintenance when conditions arise. (MSA 11.67)
The observation of the power to emerge from the seven types of false grasping; that which is both marvelous and not marvelous; and the fourfold perception. (MSA 11.68)
Equanimity toward all sentient beings, a vision of the Great Self, repaying the virtues of others, and the threefold aspiration that is uninterrupted.

From the non-abiding intention resulting from the failure to practice what was taught by the Buddha, there arises a lack of joy and a lack of exultation toward the decline or increase [of merit] among sentient beings. (MSA 11.70)
There is no lack of interest in cultivation that is merely a semblance or counterfeit;
there is no mental engagement of acquiescence, but rather a longing for that which is predicted and fixed [in liberation]. (MSA 11.71)
In the future, there is the volition for conduct arising from vision and the observation of equality;
and through conduct regarding the supreme dharmas, there is the determination of the self as supreme.
These auspicious mental orientations, which follow from the ten perfections,
indeed always serve to nourish the element of the bodhisattvas.
For the steadfast, great seeking is held to arise from nourishment and resolute intention;
it is likewise with their [seeking] that is accompanied by dwelling, free from dwelling, and sovereign.

For Bodhisattvas, there is the aspiration that is without body, the light body, and the fully perfected body; it is considered to be free from pride, characterized by subtle pride, and free from artificial construction.
In the realms of form and formlessness, dharma is the cause of characteristics; likewise, it is the cause of health.
For the wise, it is the cause of sovereignty through the superknowledges and of its own inexhaustibility.

The conceptualizations of existence and non-existence, of superimposition and denial, of unity and plurality, and of specific qualities— as well as the conceptualizations of adherence to names according to their literal meaning— should be completely abandoned by the sons of the Conqueror.
Thus, having applied intense effort with a virtuous mind and having realized the true reality of the nature of phenomena sought through the two [means],
he therefore becomes at all times a refuge for living beings, filled with qualities like the ocean.
In the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, the eleventh chapter is the "Seeking of the Dharma.
The twelfth chapter is the verse on the prohibition of stinginess regarding the teaching of the Dharma.

The wise, with joyful minds, constantly bestow upon suffering beings their lives and enjoyments—which are difficult to obtain and devoid of essence—through various forms of sublime giving. How much more so, then, do they give the noble Dharma, which is beneficial to all creatures in every way, which is never found except through hardship, and which, when bestowed, leads to increase and is inexhaustible? (MSA 12.1)

The Dharma was not taught by the Blessed One because it is to be personally realized within; yet, by means of Dharmas established through reasoning, the multitudes were drawn toward their own true nature. Then, by those whose essence is compassion—who resemble great pythons—they have been brought, as if by a mouthful of saliva, into the vast, pure, common, and inexhaustible cavity of their own tranquility. (MSA 12.2)

Therefore, that cultivation which belongs to yogins is not at all purposeless; therefore, that teaching of the Sugata is not at all purposeless. If the goal were seen through mere hearing alone, cultivation would be useless; if one were to enter into cultivation without having heard [the teachings], the teaching would be useless. (MSA 12.3)
The teaching of the supreme beings proceeds from scripture, from realization, and from mastery;
it issues forth from the mouth, from all forms, and even from space. (MSA 12.4)
This teaching of the Bodhisattvas, which is free from poison, dispels doubt, is authoritative, and reveals reality, should be understood as being twofold in its perfection. (MSA 12.5)
The teaching for the supreme beings is sweet, free from intoxication, and not wearying;
it is clear, varied, logical, intelligible, disinterested, and all-pervading.
The speech of the Son of the Victor is undepressed, sweet, well-spoken, intelligible, and likewise clear;
it is appropriate, free from ambiguity, measured, and inexhaustible.

Because it provides a summary, because it provides a detailed exposition, likewise because it conforms to the vehicles, because it is elegant, because it is intelligible, appropriate, conducive to liberation, and favorable.
This perfection of phonemes should be understood in every respect as belonging to the supreme beings;
it consists of sixty components, is inconceivable, and the voice of the Sugatas is indeed infinite.
Indeed, through speech consisting of well-joined words that resolve doubts by means of detailed instruction and analysis,
one follows the practice of extensive cultivation for those who are "those who understand through what is condensed" and "those who understand through what is elaborated."
This teaching of the Buddhas is indeed pure by virtue of the three spheres;
furthermore, it should be understood as being free from the eight faults.
Laziness, lack of understanding, failing to create the opportunity, lack of progress, not cutting through doubt, and not consolidating its removal. (MSA 12.12)
Fatigue, as well as parsimony—these are indeed considered the faults regarding discourse;
because these are absent, the teaching of the Buddhas is unsurpassed.
This sublime Dharma, being the cause of devotion, satisfaction, and wisdom,
possesses a twofold purpose, is easy to grasp, and proclaims the holy life endowed with four qualities.
Unique to others, exclusive, fulfilling the abandonment of the afflictions of the three realms,
and pure by nature as well as through the purification of stains— this is held to be the holy life (brahmavihāra) possessing these four qualities.

The intentional terminology of introduction, another intentional terminology based on characteristics, the intentional terminology of the antidote, and also the intentional terminology of transformation. (MSA 12.16)
Regarding the disciples, regarding intrinsic natures, regarding the discipline of faults,
and regarding the profundity of the expression— this intentional terminology (saṃdhi) is fourfold.
Those who perceive the essential in the non-essential, who are firmly established in error,
and who are thoroughly afflicted by defilement, attain the unsurpassed awakening.
Thus it is said.

The intention is fourfold: it should be understood as [the intention] regarding equality, regarding another meaning, furthermore regarding another time, and regarding the disposition of the person. (MSA 12.18)

Disrespect toward the Buddha and the Dharma, laziness, contentment with a mere trifle, conduct characterized by passion and pride, remorse, and instability—these constitute the divisions [of the lineage]. (MSA 12.19)
That which is an obscuration for sentient beings is the teaching of the Supreme Vehicle as its antidote;
from that, the abandonment of all faults that constitute obstacles occurs for them.
The wise one, the best of beings, who applies himself to memorizing these two verses either by way of the letter or the meaning, indeed obtains ten kinds of benefits. (MSA 12.21)
And at the time of death, there is complete nourishment of the elements and supreme joy;
furthermore, there is birth according to one's wish and the recollection of past lives in all circumstances.
Encounter with the Buddhas, hearing from them the supreme vehicle, resolute faith together with wisdom, the two gateways, and swift awakening. (MSA 12.23)

Thus, the Bodhisattva—possessing easy intelligence, tireless, compassionate, renowned for his fame, and endowed with knowledge of the proper methods—is indeed an excellent teacher; he illuminates the people through his teachings, just as the sun shines upon the world. (MSA 12.24)
In the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, the twelfth chapter is the Chapter on Teaching;
the thirteenth chapter, the Analysis of Practice, consists of six verses.
Having understood the two kinds of selflessness—of the person and of phenomena—the wise one should abandon the threefold [view] of falsity and correctness regarding these two. MSA 13.1.
One who knows the meaning of all phenomena understands their similarity to a raft;
because they have abandoned satisfaction with mere learning, they are therefore called a "knower of the Dharma."
Having thus penetrated the duality by means of ordinary knowledge,
one proceeds in accordance with the Dharma for the sake of perfecting that knowledge.
Then he attains supramundane, unsurpassed knowledge;
on the first stage, he becomes equal to all those bodhisattvas who possess that same nature.
Having brought about the complete exhaustion of all afflictions to be abandoned through vision,
one applies oneself to cultivation for the sake of abandoning the cognitive obscurations.
Accompanied by non-conceptual knowledge that establishes [the stages],
one thus practices in accordance with the Dharma throughout the remaining stages.
Easy to obtain, well-supervised, with excellent ground, with good companions, and conducive to yoga— such is the virtuous place where the wise person applies themselves.
One who is learned, has seen the truth, is eloquent, compassionate,
and untiring— such a bodhisattva should be known as a great and true person.

Having a proper object of focus, well-supported, well-sustained, and well-cultivated through skillful means, as well as being characterized by a proper application for deliverance—this is what is taught as right self-exertion. (MSA 13.9)
For the attainment of joy, the occurrence of leisure,
health, meditative concentration, and analytical discernment, the cause is indeed merit performed in the past.
Since no phenomenon exists apart from the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the Buddhas consider passion and the other afflictions to be the very means of liberation for them.
Since no phenomenon exists apart from the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu),
the wise consider this to be the intended connection (saṃdhi) regarding the teaching on affliction.
Since one correctly understands those very [afflictions] such as attachment and so forth, one is thereby liberated from them; thus, their emergence is from that [understanding].
Indeed, for the sons of the Conquerors, there is no intense suffering whatsoever that could be an obstacle, even from dwelling in the realms of hell for the sake of sentient beings;
rather, it is the various virtuous conceptualizations in the Lesser Vehicle, driven by the perceived qualities of tranquility and the defects of existence, that are obstacles for the wise.

Indeed, dwelling in the hells does not at all constitute an obstacle for the wise at any time to their stainless and vast enlightenment; however, the conceptualization of one's own welfare as supreme—even though it is cool—is an obstacle even to abiding in the state of supreme bliss in another vehicle.
The perception of the non-existence of phenomena, as well as the state of being pure despite the absence of affliction,
should be known as resembling illusions and the like, and likewise resembling space.
Just as in a painting properly executed with various colors there is no actual elevation or depression, yet it is seen;
so too, in the construction of the unreal, duality never exists in any way, yet it is always seen.
Just as when turbid water has been clarified, that clarity does not arise from elsewhere;
rather, it is merely the removal of impurities therein—such indeed is the method for the purification of one's own mind. (MSA 13.18)
The mind is held to be always luminous by nature, yet it is defiled by adventitious faults;
apart from the mind that is the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), no other mind is established as being luminous by nature.
A bodhisattva’s great love for sentient beings penetrates to the very marrow, just as it does for an only son; therefore, it is considered to always act for their benefit.
Because he acts for the benefit of sentient beings, he incurs no downfall born of attachment;
however, hatred toward any sentient being is entirely contrary to his path.
Just as a female pigeon, exceedingly affectionate toward her own offspring, remains embracing them who are her very nature,
so too does such hostility contradict one who possesses compassion for living beings, who are likewise like her own children.

Since loving-kindness exists, hostility of mind is its opposite; since peace exists, a mind of affliction is its opposite; since benefit exists, a mind of deceit is its opposite; since joy exists, fear is not its opposite. (MSA 13.23)

Just as a sick person applies himself to excellent medicine, so does he apply himself to cyclic existence; and just as a physician attends to the sick, so does he attend to sentient beings. (MSA 13.24)
Just as one behaves toward a servant who has not yet been fully trained, and just as a merchant behaves toward his own self regarding merit, so does one behave toward sensual pleasures.
Just as a washerman applies himself to his work on a garment,
so does a father behave toward his young child without causing it harm.
One who seeks fire applies himself to the lower kindling wood continuously;
or, one who is trustworthy applies himself to higher mental cultivation when it has not yet been accomplished.
Just as a magician proceeds toward his objects of knowledge through wisdom,
such is considered the practice of the bodhisattva regarding that which is to be practiced.
