Thus, constantly endowed with noble vigor and well-applied to the ripening and purification of the two,
he proceeds step by step toward supreme accomplishment through a mind that is utterly stainless and non-conceptual.
The thirteenth chapter on Practice in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra;
the fourteenth chapter, the analysis of instruction and admonition, contains these verses:
Having emerged from fifty-one incalculable eons while increasing his resolute conviction,
he is filled with wholesome qualities just as the ocean is filled with waters. (MSA 14.1)
Thus, having accumulated the necessary provisions from the very beginning, the Son of the Conqueror—
being highly wise and possessing a pliant mind— applies himself to meditative cultivation.
Then, in the stream of dharma, one receives from the Buddhas extensive instruction for the sake of attaining the vastness of tranquility and primordial wisdom.

Then, regarding the Dharma consisting of the sūtras and so forth, which reveals the non-dual meaning, the practitioner should first fix his mind upon the names of the sūtras and other such works. (MSA 14.4)
Then, he should proceed sequentially through the distinctions of the words;
he should investigate their meanings both individually and through wise reflection.
Having ascertained those meanings, he should then integrate them within the Dharma;
thereafter, he should form a firm aspiration for the realization of that meaning.
One should seek it out and examine it through a continuous stream of mental discursive thoughts,
and one should also investigate it with mental attentions that are free from such discourse and of a single flavor.
The path of calm abiding (śamatha) for this [yogin] should be known as the condensed teaching of the Dharma;
the path of insight (vipaśyanā) should be known as the investigation of the meanings of that [Dharma].
Furthermore, the path of union (yuganaddha) should be understood as the synthesis of those two;
one should seize the mind when it is sluggish and again pacify it when it is agitated.
One should maintain equanimity toward that object once it has been mastered;
then, one should again apply oneself to all [objects] continuously and with reverence.
Having bound the mind to the focal object, one should not allow it to be distracted from its flow;
quickly perceiving distraction, one should draw the mind back to that [object] once again. (MSA 14.11)
The wise person should repeatedly withdraw the mind within themselves;
thereafter, they should discipline the mind in meditative concentration by perceiving its virtues.
One should pacify aversion toward that [object] by seeing the fault of distraction;
likewise, one should pacify covetousness, dejection, and other such states when they have arisen.
Then, through that practice, the yogi further attains a state of mind that flows spontaneously, first with effort and subsequently without effort.
Then, having obtained that subtle pliancy of body and mind,
he should be known as one possessing mental application (samanaskāra), further increasing those very qualities.
Through its capacity for growth and far-reaching progression, that concentration attains stability;
purifying it for the sake of the superknowledges, it reaches supreme adaptability.

Through the accomplishment of the superknowledges within meditative absorption, he goes to world-systems for the sake of making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and for the sake of hearing [the Dharma].
Having attended upon immeasurable Buddhas for immeasurable eons,
he attains supreme adaptability of mind through that service.
Then he obtains five benefits that precede [the ultimate],
through which he becomes a vessel for purity, and subsequently attains those which are unsurpassed.
For his entire body, [even with its slight] corruption, dissolves away moment by moment;
and his body and mind are completely filled with pliancy from all sides.
He knows the appearance of all phenomena everywhere as undifferentiated;
in complete purity, he perceives the non-conceptual signs.
In every way, the wise one constantly effects the cause for the attainment and purification of the Dharma-body; thus he undertakes the gathering of causes.
Then, having become thus, that Bodhisattva, being in meditative equipoise,
does not perceive any objects as distinct from mental discourse.
For the sake of increasing the light of the Dharma, one exerts firm vigor;
and through the increase of the light of the Dharma, one abides in mind-only.
Then he perceives within the mind the appearance of all objects;
at that time, his distraction regarding the perceived object is abandoned.
Then, only the distraction of the subject remains for him;
and at that time, he again quickly touches the immediate samādhi.
Immediately after that, from which the distraction of the subject is abandoned,
these stages beginning with "Heat" (uṣmagata) are to be known in their proper sequence.
Furthermore, he attains a knowledge that is free from the grasping at duality, supramundane, unsurpassed, non-conceptual, and devoid of stains.
This transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti) is held to be his first stage;
and through immeasurable eons, it attains complete purification.

And having then realized the equality of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), one attains at all times a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, regarding them as equal to oneself. (MSA 14.30)
Regarding selflessness, the nature of suffering, what is to be done, and the absence of reward,
he maintains an even mind toward sentient beings, just like other sons of the Conqueror.
Through thoroughly purified knowledge in the sense of non-duality, one perceives the formative forces of the three realms as unreal mental constructions.
Having attained the existence of that non-existence, which is liberated from those [wrong] views, one indeed then attains the path of vision; for that reason, it is so designated.
Having understood the emptiness of non-existence, as well as the emptiness of existence,
and having understood the emptiness of intrinsic nature, one is called a knower of emptiness.
The signless state (animittapada) should be known as the complete exhaustion of conceptual constructions (vikalpa),
and unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa) is indeed the object of the wishless (apraṇihita).
O Son of the Conqueror, it is held that there is always the attainment of all the various factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa) together with that path of seeing.
Having realized through wisdom that the world is merely conditioned formations, devoid of self, and consisting only of the growth of suffering,
one abandons the view of a self which is full of harm and takes refuge in the great-souled view that possesses great purpose.
One who possesses the view of self here even without a [false] view of self, and who is deeply pained even without suffering;
who accomplishes all goals yet has no expectation of being an agent, having performed what is beneficial for himself as if for his own sake—[such a person is a bodhisattva]. (MSA 14.38)
He whose mind is liberated by supreme liberation, yet remains bound by firm and long-lasting bonds, exerts himself and acts even while not seeing the end of suffering. (MSA 14.39)
In this world, people are unable to bear even their own suffering; how much less can they bear the accumulated suffering of others?
They do not even consider a single lifetime that has passed, being indifferent to it; but the Bodhisattva is the opposite of that.

The love, the affection, the application, and the tirelessness that the sons of the Conquerors display toward sentient beings is a supreme wonder in the realms of existence; yet it is not so because they regard themselves as equal to those beings.
Thereafter, on the remaining stages of the path of cultivation,
he applies himself here to the cultivation of the two kinds of knowledge.
That gnosis is non-conceptual and purifies the qualities of a Buddha;
the other [gnosis] is established according to circumstances and brings sentient beings to maturity.
And the departure from cultivation occurs upon the completion of two incalculable aeons; having reached the final cultivation, the Bodhisattva becomes one who is consecrated.
And having attained the diamond-like concentration, which is indivisible by conceptual constructions,
one reaches the final transformation of the basis, which is free from the stains of all obscurations.
And he attains omniscience itself, the unsurpassed state,
abiding in which he acts for the benefit of all sentient beings.

How could constant vision of the Sage—whose sight is so difficult to obtain—not be of great benefit? For one whose mind is perpetually nourished by the surges of serene faith arising from incomparable hearing [of the Dharma].

Constantly urged on by the Tathāgatas face-to-face while established in the gateway to the Dharma, he is as if seized by the hair and dragged from the abyss of faults, and is forcibly established in enlightenment. (MSA 14.48)
Having completely overcome the entire world through utterly pure visions and non-conceptual awakenings,
he shines with great magnificence like a great sun, dispelling the profound darkness of the world.

The Buddhas constantly bestow perfect praise upon those who are correctly engaged in their own welfare; they offer censure to those engaged in envy, and to those intent on stability and investigation, they show the various types of factors conducive to obstacles.
Thus, in this world, the Victors duly demonstrate all kinds of dharmas to the supreme beings.
By avoiding [the former] and cultivating [the latter] in yoga, there comes to be vastness in this teaching of the Sugata.

Thus, having become fully perfected by the constant accumulation of merit and having attained the vast meditative concentration of the mind, that supreme being— having received the constant great instructions of the Sage— reaches the further shore of the ocean of virtues.
In the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra, the fourteenth chapter is the Chapter on Instruction and Admonition;
the fifteenth chapter is the Summary Verse (uddāna).

In the analysis of action accompanied by skillful means, there are four verses: Abundance of resolute belief, the seeking of the Dharma, its teaching, Practice, and likewise correct instruction and admonition. (MSA 15.1)
Just as the earth is the foundation for forests, living beings, mountains, and rivers on all sides,
so too is the threefold action of the wise toward all Buddhas described as the basis for all virtues such as generosity.

For those sons of the Conquerors who have exerted themselves through extremely difficult deeds of various forms extending over many eons, there is here no exhaustion of their actions consisting of body, speech, and mind.

Just as one who seeks his own welfare would protect his own body from poison, weapons, great fires, or enemies, so too does the Son of the Conqueror protect himself from the threefold karma and the two types of the inferior vehicle. *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* 15.4.
One who is always free from conceptual construction does not perceive the agent, the action, or the performance of the action in a threefold way.
Consequently, through the inclusion of those skillful means, that person’s action becomes infinite and reaches the further shore of purification. (MSA 15.5)
In the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, the fifteenth chapter is the "Chapter on Action Accompanied by Skillful Means.
The sixteenth chapter is the "Summary Verse on the Classification of the Perfections."
Regarding the analysis of enumeration, there are six verses:
enumeration, its definition, their sequence, etymology, and their qualities through practice; their classification, summary, opposition, known qualities, and mutual determination. (MSA 16.1)
The prosperity consisting of excellence in enjoyments, physical form, retinue, and undertakings;
as well as not being subject to the afflictions and always being free from error in one's activities.
Being well-engaged in the welfare of sentient beings, he acts through renunciation, non-injury, and forbearance;
for his own sake, he practices in every way by means of the basis, stability, and liberation.
Through non-obstruction, non-harming, endurance of harm, tireless activity, winning over others, and eloquent speech, the welfare of others becomes one's own welfare. (MSA 16.4)
Disinterest in enjoyments, intense reverence for the two [truths], lack of weariness, and non-conceptual yoga—this entire collection constitutes the supreme vehicle. (MSA 16.5)
The path of non-attachment to sense objects; another, the restraint of distractions regarding the attainment thereof;
another, the non-abandonment and increase of the quality of purity (sattva) during the purification of obscurations.
With reference to the three trainings, the Victors have fully explained the six perfections:
the first three are twofold; the last two are [twofold] from the perspective of the final two [trainings]; and one is included within all three.
Generosity is free from its opposite, accompanied by non-conceptual knowledge, fulfills all desires, and matures sentient beings in three ways. (MSA 16.8)
Ethical discipline is free from its opposites and is accompanied by non-conceptual knowledge;
it fulfills all desires and matures sentient beings in three ways.
Patience is free from its opposite and is accompanied by non-conceptual knowledge;
it fulfills all desires and matures sentient beings in three ways.
Vigor is free from its opposite, accompanied by non-conceptual knowledge, fulfills all desires, and matures sentient beings in three ways. (MSA 16.11)
Dhyāna is free from opposing factors, accompanied by non-conceptual knowledge,
fulfills all desires, and matures sentient beings in three ways.
Wisdom is free from its opposites and has reached non-conceptual knowledge;
it fulfills all desires and matures sentient beings in three ways.
The sequential explanation [of the realms] is according to their order of arising from the preceding as a support for the succeeding,
and also because of their status as inferior or superior, and as gross or subtle.
The teaching is proclaimed because of the removal of poverty, the attainment of coolness, the destruction of anger,
and the supreme knowledge of the meaning through the retention of the mind in excellent yoga.
It is taught that all [perfections] depend upon the basis of cultivation, as well as mental attention, intention, skillful means, and mastery.
The presentation of the meaning is rooted in volition;
it fulfills the twofold assistance through the perfection of enjoyments and the perfection of the personal existence.
Having fully understood that giving consists of being free from stinginess and providing for the needs of this life, material goods, and fearlessness, the wise person should practice it.
It possesses six limbs, culminates in the state of peace, bestows a happy rebirth and stability,
is firmly established, tranquil, fearless, and endowed with the equipment of merit.
Ethical discipline, which is obtained through both conventional designation and the nature of reality, exists among all those who abide in the world;
having fully understood ethical discipline in this way, the wise person should bring it to fulfillment.
The knowledge of enduring and accepting [insults] through compassion and reliance on the Dharma is said to have five benefits, and it accomplishes the welfare of both [self and others]. (MSA 16.21)
Among those, that threefold austerity is considered to be conjoined with intensity;
having thus fully understood patience, the wise person should cultivate it.
He accomplishes the welfare of both himself and another—
he who, knowing another to be angry, personally pacifies himself in that situation.
Thus it is said.
Right enthusiasm for what is wholesome is established upon faith and aspiration;
it increases qualities such as mindfulness and serves as the antidote to the afflictions.
Endowed with qualities such as non-attachment and so forth, that [vigor] is sevenfold among them;
having fully understood vigor itself, the wise person should cultivate it.
The stability of the mind within, established upon mindfulness and vigor,
leads to the attainment of bliss and mastery over the superknowledges and the meditative abodes.
Among all dharmas, meditation is preeminent, and it exists in three forms; having thus fully understood this, the wise person should cultivate it. (MSA 16.26)
Right discernment should be known as being established in meditative concentration;
it is the excellent teaching on wisdom and its livelihood for the sake of complete liberation from affliction.
Among all phenomena, there exists a superior one, and it is threefold;
having thus fully understood wisdom, the wise person should bring it to perfection.
All pure dharmas— whether distracted, concentrated, or both—
are to be understood as being embraced by two, two, and two perfections respectively.
The generosity of Bodhisattvas is neither attached, nor attached, nor attached; it is indeed not attached at all. It is neither attached, nor attached, nor attached. (MSA 16.30)
The ethical discipline of Bodhisattvas is not attached, not attached, and not attached; it is indeed unattached, not attached, not attached, and not attached. (MSA 16.31)
Neither attached, nor attached, nor attached is the patience of Bodhisattvas; it is not attachment, nor attachment, nor attachment. (MSA 16.32)
Neither attached, nor attached, nor attached; and yet it is indeed attached—such is the vigor of the bodhisattvas. Neither attached, nor attached, nor attached. (MSA 16.33)
The meditation of Bodhisattvas is neither attached, nor attached, nor attached; it is indeed not attached, neither attached, nor attached. (MSA 16.34)
The wisdom of Bodhisattvas is neither attached, nor attached, nor attached; it is not characterized by attachment. It is neither attached, nor attached, nor attached. (MSA 16.35)
The sons of the Buddha have always renounced even their own lives upon encountering a petitioner; out of compassion, they have sought neither a return favor nor a desired reward.
By that very act of giving, all people have been established in the three types of enlightenment, and through the integration of wisdom, that giving has been made inexhaustible in the world.

The sons of the Buddha have always undertaken the threefold morality consisting of restraint and exertion; heaven is not their desired goal, nor do they harbor attachment to it even when they attain it.

By that very morality, they plant all living beings in the three types of enlightenment, and through its integration with primordial wisdom, they establish that morality as inexhaustible in the world.

The sons of the Buddha have practiced patience, which is exceedingly difficult to perform, even when enduring all manner of harm from men; they do not do so for the sake of heaven, nor out of inability, nor from fear, nor with a view toward receiving benefit.

Through this unsurpassed patience, all living beings are established in the three types of enlightenment; and furthermore, through its integration with primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), patience is made inexhaustible in the world.

The sons of the Buddha have performed incomparable vigor, consisting of the application of armor, in order to destroy the host of afflictions within themselves and others, and to attain supreme enlightenment.

By that very vigor, all people have been established in the three types of enlightenment; furthermore, through its integration with primordial wisdom, that vigor has been made inexhaustible in the world.

The sons of the Buddha have fully accomplished a meditative concentration abundant in samādhis; having dwelt in all ways in the most excellent joys of dhyāna, they out of compassion have resorted to inferior births.
By that very dhyāna, they have established all people in the three types of awakening, and by means of its integration with gnosis, they have further established dhyāna as inexhaustible in the world.

The sons of the Buddha have fully understood all that is to be known together with its true nature; yet the Buddhas have produced no attachment even toward nirvāṇa, much less toward the conventional world.

By that very wisdom, they have established all living beings in the three types of enlightenment; furthermore, through their embrace of sentient beings, that wisdom has been made inexhaustible in the world.
Magnanimity, non-materiality, great purpose, and inexhaustibility—these four qualities should be understood as belonging collectively to the perfections of giving and the rest. (MSA 16.42)

The compassionate giver, through the application of excellence, overcomes the satisfaction derived from seeing [the recipient], the satisfaction of fulfilling [their wishes], the lack of satisfaction toward the beggar, and even their expectations.

Since he always renounces his life, enjoyments, and wife for the sake of sentient beings out of compassion, he rejoices exceedingly; how then could he fail to observe the restraint [of not taking what is not given]? (MSA 16.44)
How could a noble one—who is indifferent to reward, even-minded, fearless, and a giver of all things for the sake of compassion—utter a false word to harm another? (MSA 16.45)
Desiring the welfare [of others], compassionate, and extremely fearful of causing suffering to others,
he is well-engaged in the discipline of sentient beings and remains far removed from the three faults of speech.
How could he who gives everything, who is compassionate, and who is highly skilled in the arising of phenomena through dependent origination, tolerate any form of mental affliction? (MSA 16.47)
When the compassionate one perceives joy in the benefactor and always perceives the welfare of others even in suffering caused by an injurer, what is there that is not forgivable? MSA 16.48.

Because of the disappearance of the notion of "other" as distinct from "self," because of a constant love for others that exceeds [love for oneself], and because of the performance of difficult tasks—for one who possesses compassion, vigor is indeed not difficult to exert. (MSA 16.49)

For the meditation of the three [vehicles] is considered to be of little happiness, self-centered, sluggish, subject to decline, perishable, and accompanied by delusion; for Bodhisattvas, it is the opposite.
Just as objects in the dark are revealed by lamps when the darkness is dispelled, so too is the knowledge of the three [Vedas];
however, the incomparable knowledge of the compassionate ones is like the rays of the sun.
Giving is considered supreme by virtue of its basis, its object, its cause, its dedication, its motive, its knowledge, its field, and its support. (MSA 16.52)
Ethical discipline is considered supreme by virtue of its basis, its substance, its cause, its dedication, its motive, its knowledge, its field, and its support. (MSA 16.53)
It is considered supreme by reason of its basis, its substance, its sign, its dedication,
its cause, its knowledge, its field, and its support; likewise, vigor is supreme by reason of its basis, its substance, its sign, and its dedication.
It is considered supreme by reason of its cause, its knowledge, its field, and its support.
Dhyāna is considered supreme by virtue of its basis, its object, its sign, its transformation, its cause, its knowledge, its field, and its support. (MSA 16.55)
Wisdom is considered supreme by virtue of its basis, its object, its sign, its transformation, its cause, its knowledge, its field, and its support. (MSA 16.56)
A gift that brings happiness to a single being but causes harm for many eons would still be dear to Bodhisattvas; how much more so its opposite?
The very wealth that embodied beings desire for their own sake, the wise bestow upon other beings;
that which people seek as wealth for the sake of the body, that same thing is bestowed by the wise hundreds of times over.

When the mind does not suffer even as one abandons the very body, what need is there to mention inferior wealth? That his joy is thus extraordinary is because that [wealth] is superior to it. MSA 16.59.

Even a seeker does not attain such satisfaction through receiving desired and cherished gifts as the wise one attains here through the gift of all his possessions by means of satisfying those who seek them.
Even a beggar does not regard himself as wealthy in the same way that one with full enjoyments regards oneself;
however, through the gift of all that he possesses, the wise person, though possessing nothing, regards himself as truly wealthy.
Even upon obtaining vast wealth, the seeker does not consider it a favor received from the donor for the sake of profit;
rather, having satisfied the seekers here with excellent gifts according to the rule, the wise one regards them as having rendered him a great service.

Those embodied beings who, their own grief having vanished, remain in a state of well-being and enjoy even his vast wealth—just as travelers enjoy the abundant fruits of a tree of enjoyment along the road—he is none other than the Bodhisattva, who delights in extensive giving and supreme enjoyment. (MSA 16.63)

Vigor is taught as that which is to be fully understood through its preeminence, its causes, its classification by action, its distinction of modes, its distinction of bases, and its distinction as the antidote to the four obstructions. (MSA 16.64)
Vigor is supreme among the collection of pure qualities, for it is by depending upon it that they are subsequently attained.
Through vigor, there is an immediately blissful dwelling, as well as the accomplishment of both supramundane and worldly goals.
Through vigor, one attains the desired enjoyments of existence; through vigor, one achieves powerful purity;
through vigor, having transcended the view of a self-identity, one is liberated; and through vigor, one awakens to supreme enlightenment.
Furthermore, vigor is considered to be that which involves decrease and increase, that which masters liberation, and another which consists of the favorable side and its opposite;
that which has entered into reality, that which is transformative, that which is of great purpose, and another is explained as etymological.

The Buddhas proclaim that there are four kinds of vigor in every respect: first, the vigor of armor; then, the vigor of application properly exerted; as well as the unflagging, unshakable, and insatiable vigor.

Based on the support of persons engaged in the three vehicles, there is another [type of] vigor—inferior, middling, and superior—which, through the application of a sluggish or exceedingly noble intention and intellect, is considered to have small or great purpose. (MSA 16.69)
The energetic one is not defeated by enjoyments; the energetic one is not defeated by the afflictions.
The energetic one is not defeated by weariness; the energetic one is not defeated by failure to attain.
The definitive determination of the six perfections should be understood in every respect through their mutual inclusion, their classification, their nature, and their signs. (MSA 16.71)

Generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and consistency between words and deeds are intended [as the four means of attraction] through their teaching, their instigation, and one's own conformity to them. (MSA 16.72)
It should be known that there are four types [of skillful means] according to the four bases of sympathy: the benevolent, the receptive, the engaging, and likewise the conforming.
By the first, one becomes a fit vessel; by the second, there is resolute conviction;
by the third, there is practice; and by the fourth, purification. (MSA 16.74)
The state of having the four means of attraction is considered to result from two types of gathering:
through material things and through the Dharma; and through the Dharma by way of the object and so forth.
Gathering [beings] is generally to be understood as inferior, middling, or superior, as fruitless or fruitful, and indeed as fruitful in every respect, according to the distinction of its forms.
This method is resorted to by those engaged in attracting the assembly;
it is praised as a skillful means for the easy accomplishment of all goals for everyone.
Those who have been gathered, those who will be gathered, and those who are being gathered now—all of them are thus; therefore, that path is for the ripening of sentient beings.
Thus, with a mind constantly unattached to enjoyments, having reached the further shore of tranquility, self-restraint, and exertion, established in the self,
and free from conceptual construction regarding the causes of existence and sense objects, he becomes a gatherer of the multitude of beings.
The sixteenth chapter, the Section on the Perfections, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* is completed.
The seventeenth chapter, the Analysis of Worship of the Buddha, consists of seven verses.
Worship of the Buddhas, whether in their presence or in their absence, with robes and other offerings,
by one whose mind is deeply serene, serves to fulfill the two accumulations.
For one who possesses the vow and for whom the birth of a Buddha is not fruitless,
the non-apprehension of the triad constitutes the perfected worship of the Buddha.
Another [perfection] is for the sake of maturing immeasurable sentient beings;
another is through material gifts and through the mind; and another is through resolute belief and through the foundation.
And another [type of patience] arises from compassionate concern and forbearance in one's conduct;
furthermore, it arises from the engagement with objects, from awakening, from liberation, and from suchness.
Worship is demonstrated by way of its basis, its substance, its cause, its transformation, its motive, its field, and its support. (MSA 17.5)
It is twofold by way of cause and fruit, by oneself and by others, and also by way of gain and honor, and by way of practice. (MSA 17.6)
Worship is considered to be limited or extensive, with or without pride,
and it is regarded as such according to its application, its course, and its aspiration.

Supreme worship toward the Buddhas arises from one’s own mind through: inclination toward the Dharma, the resolute intention, mastery, the embrace of non-conceptual means, and the entry into the state where all activities are of a single purpose. (MSA 17.8)
Service is demonstrated by way of its basis, its object, its motive, its dedication, its cause, its knowledge, its field, and its support. (MSA 17.9)

One should rely upon a friend who is self-controlled, tranquil, and thoroughly pacified; who is superior in virtue, diligent, and rich in scriptural knowledge; who has awakened to reality, is endowed with eloquence, is compassionate by nature, and is free from weariness.
A wise person should serve a spiritual friend with honors, gains, and personal attendance, as well as through correct practice;
possessing an intention that understands the Dharma as it truly is, they should approach the friend at the proper time with humility.
Free from longing for honor and gain, he should dedicate that [merit] toward spiritual practice;
and by practicing according to the instructions, the wise one should thereby please the Teacher's mind.
"Having attained skill in the three vehicles through wisdom, one should strive for the accomplishment of one's own vehicle alone.
Thus, from skill in the three vehicles arises knowledge; [it is applied] for the sake of maturing immeasurable sentient beings and for the realization of a pure field. (MSA 17.13)

Endowed with the quality of being an heir to the teachings rather than to material things, the wise one should not enter into friendship for the sake of gain; rather, he should serve a friend both outwardly and inwardly by following the Dharma through its causes, its fruits, and its gateways.

A wise person should indeed rely upon a spiritual friend through the hearing of the teachings, through mental application, through the cultivation of a mind free from pride, through the practice of the [right] course, and through the power of aspiration. (MSA 17.15)
The supreme service to true friends arises from one’s own mind through: inclination toward the Dharma, intention, and the [ten] masteries;
through being embraced by non-conceptual means; and through entering into the state of having a single common task with all.
The Brahmās have abandoned their opposites and have attained non-conceptual knowledge;
they function with respect to the three kinds of objects and are the ripeners of sentient beings, O steadfast one.

For those seeking happiness, those afflicted by suffering, those who are happy, and those who are distressed, as well as for the wise regarding the Dharma taught to them and its suchness, these [perfections] proceed.
And because it has suchness as its object, because of the attainment of patience,
because of purification, because of two types of action, and also because of the destruction of the afflictions, loving-kindness is without objective support.
They are both immovable and moving, tasted by the wretched, yet they are not to be known [as such]; for Bodhisattvas are established in the immovable, which are free from attachment.

Those whose nature is unconcentrated, those who are weak or middling, those belonging to inferior stages, those with inferior intentions, and those who are equal [to them]—these are indeed inferior; otherwise, they are superior.
When the wise one, having dwelt in the Brahma-abodes, is born among those subject to desire,
he thereby fulfills the accumulations and matures sentient beings.

And everywhere he is never separated from the sublime states (brāhmavihāra) and is free from their opposites; even when confronted by intense conditions for them, he does not undergo transformation, even if he should become heedless.
For a bodhisattva who is possessed of ill-will and harmfulness, as well as discontent, ill-will, and sensual desire,
encounters many kinds of misfortune.
Through the afflictions, one destroys oneself, harms sentient beings, and violates moral discipline;
one is accompanied by remorse, deprived of gain, and likewise lacks protection from the Teacher.

One who possesses a basis for transgression and lacks the intention [to abandon it] is reborn in the unfavorable states; having lost both what was attained and what was not yet attained, he experiences great suffering in his mind.
All these faults do not occur for one who is well-established in loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables].
Unafflicted, they do not abandon cyclic existence for the sake of sentient beings.

Even toward an only son who possesses every virtue, all sentient beings do not possess such an intention of loving-kindness and so forth as that which the sons of the Conquerors have toward all beings. (MSA 17.28)
[He sees beings] aflame, under the power of enemies, overcome by suffering, enveloped in darkness,
set upon difficult paths, and bound with great fetters.
He feels compassion for sentient beings who are weak, who are greedy for great food mixed with poison, who have lost their way, and who have set out upon a wrong path.

For the son of the Conqueror who relies on this Dharma—which removes obstacles, is the seed of supreme enlightenment, brings happiness, is the cause for attaining peace, and bestows one's own true nature—enlightenment is not far off. (MSA 17.31)
Having realized that the entire cycle of existence is of the nature of suffering and devoid of self,
the compassionate one of supreme intelligence neither falls into agitation nor is afflicted by defects.

Observing the world as being of the nature of suffering, the compassionate one feels sorrow and understands it as it truly is; furthermore, he does not experience weariness even in the future regarding the means for its avoidance.

This fourfold compassion of those whose nature is compassion arises from its natural disposition and from analytical reflection; it is preceded by the practice of its cultivation, is free from opposing factors, and is attained through purification. (MSA 17.34)

That is not compassion which is not equal or constant, or which does not arise from the resolute intention, or from practice, or from detachment, or from non-apprehension; for one who is thus is not a compassionate bodhisattva.
Compassion, patience, reflection, aspiration, birth, and the maturation of sentient beings—
this is the great tree of compassion, beginning with the root and ending with the flowers, leaves, and final fruit.
If compassion were not the root, there would be no endurance of difficult practices;
and a wise person who cannot endure suffering would never contemplate the welfare of sentient beings. (MSA 17.37)
One whose intellect is devoid of reflection would not make a vow for future births in the pure realms;
failing to attain such auspicious births, one could never bring sentient beings to maturity.

Compassion is the watering; loving-kindness is its nourishment through the happiness found in that suffering. The extensive growth of its branches should be understood as arising from thorough mental attention. (MSA 17.39)
Through the relinquishing and taking up of leaves, through the non-interruption of the continuum of vows,
and through the accomplishment of the two kinds of conditions, from this [tree] there arises fruitful blossoming and fruit.
Who would not feel compassion for sentient beings, who possess the quality of great mercy, since even in suffering they experience incomparable happiness born of that very compassion? (MSA 17.41)

The minds of the compassionate do not abide in tranquility when they are moved by pity for those who are afflicted; how much less could they have any attachment to worldly happiness or even to their own lives? (MSA 17.42)
That affection which is blameless and yet not worldly does not exist;
however, the affection of compassion among the wise is blameless and transcends the world.
How could that means which is intended to uplift the world—resting as it does in the great flood of suffering and the profound darkness of ignorance—not be irreproachable? (MSA 17.44)
That affection does not exist in the world among Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, let alone among others; how then could it not be supramundane?
In the absence of suffering, that suffering which arises for Bodhisattvas through compassion terrifies them at first; yet once experienced, it brings intense joy.
What is more marvelous than this: that worldly suffering, born of compassion, overcomes all happiness—even for one who is liberated and has accomplished his purpose? (MSA 17.47)
The gift accompanied by compassion produces for the steadfast that bliss of giving which the enjoyments of the three realms do not touch even in a fraction.
Because of compassion, he does not abandon the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which consists of suffering, for the sake of sentient beings;
for what suffering that brings benefit to others has not been undertaken by those possessed of compassion? (MSA 17.49)
For one who possesses compassion, compassion, generosity, and enjoyments always increase;
and from this, there arises happiness produced by affection, assistance, and that [compassion's] power.
"I grow, and I cause others to grow; I bring them to maturity in generosity, I bring them happiness, I attract them, and I lead them"—thus does compassion speak, as it were, to those who are weary.
Suffering when others suffer out of compassion, by what means could one be happy without bestowing happiness upon them?
Therefore, the compassionate person makes himself happy by bestowing happiness upon others. (MSA 17.52)
The compassionate teacher, always desiring no happiness for himself, instructs his own gift thus:
"Make others happy with enjoyments, or else let me too share in that happiness. (MSA 17.53)
That fruitful gift was given by me to sentient beings, sharing their happiness as my own;
if you have any obligation toward me, may its fruit ripen for them alone to their heart's content.
For one who hates enjoyments, enjoyments approach even more abundantly and auspiciously when given away;
for I do not consider that to be true happiness, since I am intent upon the successive transmission of giving.
Since you constantly look upon me with compassion even as I relinquish everything that exists, surely you must know by this that you have no desire for the fruits of my actions.
If I were to obtain the fruit of that [giving], I would not fail to relinquish it;
for one who delights in giving does not remain without giving for even a single moment. (MSA 17.57)
Since you do not bear fruit for that which has not been done, it is not equal to me in my expectation of a return;
however, since you yield fruit for another without regard for a return, let it be as you wish.
The compassionate giving of the Sons of the Conquerors is irreproachable, pure, beneficial, protective, unsearchable, and unstained. (MSA 17.59)
The gift of the sons of the Conquerors is complete, vast, excellent, constant, joyful, disinterested, pure, inclined toward awakening, and inclined toward virtue. (MSA 17.60)
A person who possesses enjoyments does not obtain such satisfaction from their use as a compassionate one, whose mind is nourished by the threefold happiness, attains through renunciation.
Compassion for the wretched, compassion for the fierce, compassion for the agitated, compassion for those who are heedless,
compassion for those dependent on sense objects, and compassion for those who are wrongly attached.
The compassion of Bodhisattvas arises from happiness, from suffering, and from that which follows them;
the compassion of Bodhisattvas arises from its cause, from friends, and from its own nature.
The compassion of Bodhisattvas should be known as equal due to their intention, their practice, their detachment, their non-apprehension, and their purity. (MSA 17.64)

The supreme cultivation of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] arises from one's own mind, from the Dharma, and from resolute conviction; it also arises from intention, from mastery, from non-conceptuality, and from unity. (MSA 17.65)

Thus, having conceived profound faith in the Blessed One, making great offerings of material requisites, constant respect, and food, and always serving virtuous friends who bring benefit, one who has compassion for the world attains all accomplishments. (MSA 17.66)
The seventeenth chapter, "Worship, Service, and the Immeasurables," in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, is completed.
The eighteenth chapter, "The Analysis of Shame," consists of sixteen verses.

In the steadfast one, shame is free from its opposites, has reached non-conceptual knowledge, has as its object that which is inferior yet irreproachable, and brings sentient beings to maturity. (MSA 18.1)
For the wise, shame arises from laziness in practicing the six perfections, as well as from engaging in qualities that are conducive to the afflictions. (MSA 18.2)

Shame that is of an unconcentrated nature, moderate, belonging to a lower stage, characterized by a low aspiration, and shared with others is indeed inferior; however, if it is otherwise, it is superior. (MSA 18.3)
The wise one who lacks a sense of shame tolerates the afflictions through improper reflection;
harboring resentment, indifference, and pride, he harms both sentient beings and his own ethical discipline.
Due to remorse, one becomes dejected and suffers a loss of honor;
consequently, one is disregarded by the assembly of faithful humans and by the Teacher. (MSA 18.5)
He is censured by his fellow sons of the Conqueror, he incurs ill repute in the world,
and in this very life, he is born again and again deprived of favorable conditions.
Because he undergoes the loss of both attained and unattained wholesome dharmas,
he dwells in suffering and consequently falls into a state of mental unease.
All these faults exist among those who possess coldness, but not among the sons of the Conqueror;
the wise one is always born among gods and humans.
Through a sense of shame, that wise son of the Conqueror quickly fulfills the accumulations for enlightenment and does not become weary of maturing sentient beings.
He is born constantly both free from adverse factors and not devoid of their remedies;
thus does the son of the Conqueror endowed with a sense of shame obtain this benefit.
For the fool is defiled by faults even when well-concealed by fine garments due to a lack of shame;
whereas the Son of the Victor, though without garments, is clothed in shame and is thus freed from the stain of faults.
Like space, the son of the Victor who possesses a sense of shame is unstained by worldly phenomena;
adorned with shame, he shines when in the company of other sons of the Victor.
For Bodhisattvas, a sense of shame (*hrī*) toward those to be trained is like a mother’s affection;
furthermore, for those wandering in cyclic existence, shame is a protection against all faults.

The absence of acquiescence toward all [faults], the engagement in acquiescence toward all [virtues], and the engagement in all [wholesome actions]—this is the mark of one possessed of shame, as ordained by shame. (MSA 18.14)

The cultivation of moral shame (*hrī*) is preeminent by virtue of one's own mind, through resolute conviction in the Dharma, through intention, through mastery, through non-conceptuality, and also through unity. (MSA 18.15)
The fortitude of Bodhisattvas is distinguished from all others by its characteristics, its classifications, and its firmness. (MSA 18.16)
Vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as truthfulness, steadfastness, and fortitude,
are considered [the qualities] from which the Bodhisattva proceeds, being fearless because of these three.

Fear arises from sluggishness, from agitation, and from delusion regarding one's duties; therefore, the designation "steadfastness" (dhṛti) should be understood as applying to one's own threefold [qualities].
By nature, in their aspiration, and in their very lack of dependence, as well as toward the misconduct of sentient beings and upon hearing of profundity and magnanimity— MSA 18.19.
Regarding the difficulty of disciplining those to be trained, the inconceivability of the Victor’s body, various difficult feats, and the non-abandonment of cyclic existence; (MSA 18.20)
And in that very state which is free from affliction, steadfastness arises for the wise one;
it is unequalled compared to others, since he is therefore considered the foremost among those possessed of steadfastness.
The hero does not tremble at evil friends, suffering, or the hearing of the profound, just as Mount Sumeru is unmoved by locusts, the wind of their wings, or the oceans. (MSA 18.22)
The indefatigability of Bodhisattvas is peerless in three matters:
insatiability regarding what is heard, great vigor, and [endurance] toward suffering; it is based upon a sense of shame and moral dread.
Intense aspiration for great enlightenment and tirelessness are considered the qualities of the wise;
they are unperfected, perfected, and well-perfected across the stages.
It is distinguished by its subject matter, its scope, its activity, its characteristics, its inexhaustibility, and the attainment of its fruit. (MSA 18.25)
For the wise, knowledge of the treatises consists of the gateways of meditative concentration and the dhāraṇīs;
once mastered, they serve for the ripening of sentient beings and for the preservation of the true Dharma.
Indeed, the world-knowledge of the wise, which is peerless in terms of body, speech, and the knowledge of reality, excels that of all others.
Furthermore, for what purpose is this? He says: "For the sake of making sentient beings vessels. For what purpose, for the sake of being vessels? "For the practice of the true Dharma" (MSA 18.28).
Since the repeated arising of the world is desired from the two truths,
and its cessation is from those two, one who knows that is called a knower of the world.
For the sake of their pacification and attainment, the wise one applies himself to the truths;
for it is because he possesses knowledge of the truths that the wise one is indeed defined as "one who knows the world."
The Dharma of the teaching is that of the ṛṣis; its meaning is intentional;
it is authoritative and of definitive meaning; and its attainment is beyond verbal expression.

In this context, the negation is taught regarding the rejection of what has been stated, regarding that which is falsely conceived, and regarding the attainment of that which is accompanied by desire.
Through resolute belief, through investigation, through hearing correctly from others,
and even through non-conceptual knowledge, there is indeed no loss for the wise.
The four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) of the bodhisattvas are peerless;
they are considered such because of their knowledge regarding synonyms, characteristics, speech, and cognition. (MSA 18.34)
For one engaged in teaching, there is that which is taught and that by which it is taught;
the teaching of both the phenomenon (dharma) and its meaning (artha) is accomplished through speech and through knowledge alone.

The four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) arise from the brief statement and detailed explanation of the Dharma, from the complete attainment of both [the meaning and the expression] in every way, and from the thorough knowledge and abandonment of objections. (MSA 18.36)
Having attained internal equanimity, that subsequent realization which serves to destroy all doubts is called the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
The equipment of the Bodhisattvas consists of merit and wisdom; it is peerless.
One leads to prosperity within saṃsāra, while the other pertains to wandering through existence without affliction.
Generosity and ethical discipline are the accumulation of merit; wisdom is the accumulation of knowledge.
Three other [perfections] serve both; all five are also the accumulation of knowledge.
That which is the nourishment for virtue, attained through continuous cultivation again and again,
is the equipment that accomplishes all goals for the wise one.
The accumulation for the wise is gathered for the sake of entry, for the signless, for effortlessness, for consecration, and for the ultimate goal.
The cultivation of the applications of mindfulness occurs through fourteen aspects;
because it is unequaled for the wise, it excels all others.
It is distinguished by way of its basis, its antidote, and likewise its entry; as well as by its object, its mental attention, and its attainment.

Through conformity and following after, through thorough knowledge and arising, through measure and through supremacy, there is another [type of perfection] due to the attainment of cultivation. (MSA 18.44)
The right exertions of the wise are unequaled by all embodied beings; they are cultivated as the antidote to the defects of the [four] foundations of mindfulness.
In the enjoyment of cyclic existence and in the abandonment of the hindrances,
in the relinquishing of mental attention and in the entry into the stages.
In the dwelling in the signless, in the attainment of the prophecy,
in the ripening of sentient beings, and in the empowerment of the wise.
For the sake of purifying the field and for the attainment of the ultimate goal,
the cultivation of the remedies for the opposing factors is practiced by the Bodhisattvas.
Relying upon desire, the cultivation of yoga accompanied by signs is declared to be the antidote in all the right abandonments.
And the four bases of miraculous power, which are the preeminent characteristics of the wise, arise for the accomplishment of all goals, both for oneself and for others. (MSA 18.50)
The establishment of the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) for the wise is intended in every respect by way of their basis, their differentiation, their means, and their accomplishment. (MSA 18.51)
Relying upon the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā), fourfold differentiation,
as well as means (upāya) and sixfold accomplishment (abhinirhāra), are prescribed.
The first is that of application, the second is that of favoring,
the third is that of binding, and the fourth is that of counteracting.
The accomplishment of vision, of instruction, of the play of stability,
of the power of aspiration, and of the attainment of the Dharma.
In this context, enlightenment, conduct, learning, tranquility,
and insight should be known as the basis for faith and the other [faculties], according to their respective roles in accomplishing the goal.
Furthermore, faith and the other [faculties], when they have entered the stages and are free from defilement,
are designated as "powers" because their opposing factors have become weak.
The establishment of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) is prescribed for one who has entered the [first] stage,
because of the further realization of the equality of all phenomena and of all sentient beings.
Mindfulness operates everywhere for the sake of conquering the unconquered among the objects of knowledge; and his investigation is for the sake of shattering all conceptual constructions and signs.
Just as the precious elephant is for the defeat of adversaries,
so too does vigor proceed toward swift and complete awakening;
and through the increase of the light of the Dharma, one is certainly filled with joy.
Through liberation from all hindrances, one attains bliss by means of pliancy;
and the fulfillment of intended aims arises from meditative concentration.
Through equanimity, he dwells everywhere according to his wish;
being always supreme, he dwells with the non-conceptual attainment subsequent to [meditative concentration] and with conceptualization.
A Bodhisattva endowed with such qualities proceeds like a universal monarch (cakravartin),
constantly surrounded by the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) which are like the seven precious jewels.
The limb of reliance, the limb of essential nature, and the third, the limb of departure;
the fourth is the limb of benefit, and the limb of non-affliction consists of three parts.
And following after awakening as it truly is arises thereafter;
the establishment according to awakening and the entry into that established state [are likewise attained]. (MSA 18.64)

And there is the purification of the three types of karma, the cultivation of the antidote, [the purification] of the obscuration to the knowable, of the path, and of the extraordinary qualities. (MSA 18.65)
Through the mind abiding in the mind and through the discernment of phenomena, one relies upon right stability; thus there arise calm abiding and insight.
It is considered to be universal, partial,
and the proximate cause for penetration, for departure, for the signless, and for the unconditioned.
In both the purified and the completely pure [stages], calm abiding and insight pertain to all levels; for the steadfast one, that yoga is the accomplisher of everything.

One attains skill in fulfilling the qualities of a Buddha, in maturing sentient beings, in the swift attainment [of the goal], in the purity of activity, and in the non-interruption of the path. (MSA 18.69)
The skill in means of the bodhisattvas on all the stages is peerless;
relying upon this skill, they accomplish all goals.
Through the ripening [of karma], through the practice of hearing, and through meditative concentration, there is also retention (dhāraṇī);
it may be small or great, and that which is great is further of three kinds.
For the wise who have not yet entered or have entered [the path], it is weak or middling;
for those on the impure stages, it is indeed great, while for those on the pure stages, it is vast.
Relying upon that dhāraṇī, Bodhisattvas repeatedly proclaim the true Dharma and perpetually uphold it. (MSA 18.73)
Volition conjoined with desire and impelled by knowledge—
this is indeed the vow of the wise, which is peerless across all stages.
It should be understood as being both the cause and the immediate fruit;
it serves to accomplish one's aims in the future through the fulfillment [of wishes] arising from mind alone.
Wondrous, great, and pure, on each successive stage up to enlightenment, it accomplishes the welfare of both oneself and others for bodhisattvas.
The two kinds of selflessness should be known as the basis for the grasping at a self,
and their perpetual pacification is the objective domain of the three concentrations.
Samādhi should be known as threefold, according to the nature of the grasped and the grasper:
it is non-conceptual, turned away [from objects], and always endowed with delight. (MSA 18.78)
The threefold purpose of the concentrations on emptiness and so forth is proclaimed for the sake of full comprehension, abandonment, and furthermore, for direct realization.
The four summaries of the Dharma have been taught to the bodhisattvas as the secret foundation of meditative concentration, out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings.

For the wise, these four refer to the meaning of non-existence, the meaning of non-conceptualization, the meaning of mere imagination, and the meaning of the cessation of conceptualization. (MSA 18.81)

Because of non-connection, because of arising from a cause, because of contradiction, because of not remaining by itself, because of non-existence, because of the exclusivity of the definition, because of following along, and because of cessation. (MSA 18.82)
And because transformation is perceived, because it is both cause and fruit,
because of being appropriated and because of sovereignty, and because of following after pure beings.

The first [type of transformation] occurs through degrees of intensity, through accumulation, through the state of its basis, through modification and maturation, and likewise through being inferior or superior.
Arising occurs through luminosity and non-luminosity, by going to another location,
by being with seed or without seed, and as a reflected image.

Because there is no cause for the fourteenfold arising [of the aggregates], because accumulation and so forth are untenable, and because it is impossible for them to serve as a basis, [the self does not exist]. (MSA 18.86)
Because that which is established cannot cease at the end, and because there is no transformation due to the non-destruction of the beginning;
likewise, this applies to the inferior and the superior, as well as to the luminous and the non-luminous.
Because there is no going, because staying is impossible, because a final state is inconceivable,
and because the mind continues in succession, all conditioned phenomena are momentary.
The momentariness of the sixfold objects of the elements is established because of their drying up and increasing,
because of their inherent mobility, and because of their waxing and waning.
Because it arises from that [earth], because it is a fourfold transformation of earth,
and because its color, odor, taste, and touch are identical, it is likewise [earth].
Because its existence depends on fuel, because it is perceived as having degrees of intensity,
because it follows the mind, and because of [the Buddha's] questioning, external objects are therefore also momentary.
The person (pudgala) should be described as existing as a designation, but not as a substantial entity;
because it is not perceived, because it is a misconception, because it is a defilement, and because its cause is defiled. (MSA 18.92)
Therefore, it cannot be described as either identical to or different from [the aggregates], because of those two faults;
furthermore, because it would follow that the aggregates are the self, and it would follow that the self is a substantial entity.
If it were a substantial entity yet inexpressible, there would have to be a purpose for its being expressed;
however, that which is inexpressible in terms of identity or difference cannot be tenable if it lacks such a purpose.
Neither from the perspective of defining characteristics, nor from worldly observation, nor even from scripture,
is it tenable that fuel and fire are inexpressible [as identical or different], for they are perceived as a duality.
And since consciousness arises when there is a duality, that [self] is not a condition;
therefore, from the perspective of being purposeless, it is not tenable for anything from the seer up to the liberator to exist.
If there were ownership, one would not engage in that which is impermanent and undesirable;
thus, the definition of karma as something to be accomplished is sublated in three ways by perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, the effort for seeing and so forth is not self-originated even from the three [causes];
moreover, seeing and so forth would be effortless if they were dependent upon such effort.
Because it is not an agent, because it is impermanent, and because its activity occurs only occasionally rather than constantly,
it is not logical for effort in seeing and other such functions to be self-existent.
For that which remains as such, for that which has perished, and because of prior non-existence and impermanence,
as well as due to the absence of a third alternative, its status as a condition is not tenable.
All phenomena are without self; in the ultimate sense, they are emptiness.
Furthermore, it is precisely because of this that the fault in perceiving a self has been taught.
Regarding defilement and purification, as well as their distinct states and divisions,
the distinctions in activity and continuity are indeed demonstrated by means of the person (pudgala).
The view of a self would not be produced; practice would be beginningless;
there would be effortless liberation for all, or else there would be no liberation at all, nor would a person exist.

The person (pudgala) should be said to exist as a conceptual designation (prajñapti), but not substantially (dravyataḥ). Therefore, it cannot be described as either identical to or different from the aggregates (skandha); for otherwise, it would follow that the aggregates themselves are the self, or that the person possesses substantial reality.
If it were ineffable as a substance and so forth, its purpose would have to be stated;
yet it is not logical for it to be ineffable in terms of identity or difference while being devoid of purpose.
Neither from the perspective of defining characteristics, nor from worldly observation, nor even from the scriptures is such a position tenable.
The fuel and the fire cannot be said [to be identical or different], because they are perceived as a duality;

for consciousness arises in dependence upon these two, and thus that [fire] is not the causal condition [of the fuel]. Moreover, if it were the master [of the fuel], it would not set forth that which is impermanent and undesirable.
Furthermore, it is illogical for vision and the other faculties to be independent of effort,
since they lack an agent, are impermanent, and would otherwise function simultaneously and eternally; thus,
the self-arising of effort in vision and the rest is not tenable.
For that which remains as such, for that which has perished, because of prior non-existence, because of impermanence,
and because of the absence of a third alternative, its status as a condition is not tenable.
All phenomena are selfless; from the ultimate perspective, they are emptiness, and it is precisely because of this that the fault in perceiving a self has been taught.
Regarding affliction and purification, which are distinguished by their different states and divisions,
the distinction between their activity and continuum is indeed demonstrated by means of the person (pudgala).
The view of a self is not to be produced, because it has already arisen from the very beginning;
nor is it for the sake of practicing it, because the practice of the view of a self is beginningless.
And if liberation were taught as occurring through the view of a self,
then in that case, liberation would be effortless for everyone.
Thus, always endowed with these qualities, Bodhisattvas do not neglect their own welfare and they accomplish the welfare of others.
The eighteenth chapter, the Section on the Factors Conducive to Enlightenment, in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, is completed.
Regarding the nineteenth section, the Analysis of Marvels, there are three verses.
The renunciation of one's own body and even of prosperity when they are present; and patience toward the weak, being indifferent toward both body and life—[these are the marks of a bodhisattva].

The undertaking of vigor, the absence of relish for meditative concentrations, and indeed the very happiness therein, as well as non-conceptuality regarding wisdom—this is the marvelous path of the wise. (MSA 19.2)
Birth in the family of the Tathāgatas, the receipt of the prophecy,
the attainment of empowerment, and the realization of awakening are considered the marvels.
Having cultivated dispassion, compassion, and even the supreme meditative absorption,
as well as equanimity of mind— it is not surprising that they are thus endowed with these qualities.
The affection that wise beings feel for sentient beings is not surpassed by the affection they feel for themselves, their wives, their children, their friends, or their kinsmen. (MSA 19.5)

Impartiality toward those in need, the constant non-violation of ethical discipline, patience in all circumstances for the sake of sentient beings, and the undertaking of great vigor as well. (MSA 19.6)
Dhyāna that is always wholesome and wisdom that is non-conceptual—
these should be understood as the equanimity of mind toward those very [qualities] possessed by Bodhisattvas.
Establishing [others] in the state of being a vessel, planting them in the very precepts, enduring harm, and engaging in activity for the sake of others. (MSA 19.8)
Winning [beings] over to this teaching, cutting through their doubts, and acting for the benefit of sentient beings— this is held to be the mark of the wise.
Those who, with an impartial intention, always uphold [the teachings] for the sake of sentient beings,
cause them to be born on the noble stages and cause them to increase through wholesome qualities.
They protect [beings] from misdeeds and cause them to master the scriptures;
through these five activities, the sons of the Conquerors are like mothers to sentient beings. (MSA 19.11)
Because they always plant faith in all sentient beings, and because they enjoin them to the higher training in ethics and so forth, as well as to liberation. (MSA 19.12)
Through these five activities— soliciting the Buddhas and abandoning their obscurations— the sons of the Victors are like fathers to sentient beings.
They indeed conceal from sentient beings that which is not fit to be taught;
they censure failure in the training and praise its perfection.
They bestow instruction and indeed make the Māras known;
through these five activities, the sons of the Victors are like kinsmen to sentient beings.
With their own intellects untiring regarding both affliction and purification,
they bestow all worldly prosperity as well as that which transcends the world.
Those who always desire the happiness and welfare [of others] are inseparable from them because they never grow weary;
through these five activities, the sons of the Victors are like friends to sentient beings. (MSA 19.17)
Those who are always diligent in bringing sentient beings to maturity, who speak of the correct way to liberation, and who are patient toward misconduct; MSA 19.18.
The sons of the Victors, skilled in the means for that [attainment], bestow the two kinds of perfection; by these five activities, they are like servants to sentient beings. (MSA 19.19)

Those who are considered to have attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) are the instructors of all vehicles and the ones who establish others in the yoga of accomplishment.
With pleasant countenances, and indifferent toward both recompense and karmic maturation,
the sons of the Conquerors are like teachers of sentient beings through these five types of action.
Those who are dedicated to the welfare of sentient beings fulfill the accumulations;
having fulfilled them, they swiftly liberate others and cause the abandonment of opposing factors.

Through five types of actions, the sons of the Victors—resembling spiritual preceptors for sentient beings—unite them with the diverse worldly prosperities as well as with the supramundane. (MSA 19.23)
Through non-attachment to enjoyments, by not violating moral discipline, through devotion to gratitude, and by application to correct practice; MSA 19.24.
For embodied beings who abide precisely in the six perfections become, in that way, benefactors in return to the Bodhisattvas.
They always desire the increase and decrease [of merit], the maturation of sentient beings,
the progress through the stages, and unsurpassed enlightenment.
In the abandoning of fear, in the generation [of the thought of awakening], in the cutting off of doubt,
and in the instruction on practice, the sons of the Conquerors are always unfailing.
Generosity without expectation of reward and free from longing for rebirth;
ethical discipline and patience in all circumstances; and vigor in the arising of all that is wholesome.

Likewise, the meditative concentration excluding the formless [attainments], and wisdom conjoined with skillful means, constitute the correct application of the wise in the six perfections. (MSA 19.29)
Attachment to enjoyments, having flaws, pride, seeking mere pleasure, relishing [meditative states], and conceptualization are the causes of decline for the wise. (MSA 19.30)
For those Bodhisattvas who abide in those very antidotes,
the factors conducive to distinction are to be known as arising from the opposite of these [hindrances].
Deceiving others by feigning departure, displaying a pleasant countenance, acting out of greed, and likewise maintaining stillness of speech and body; MSA 19.32.
Perfection in eloquent speech devoid of correct practice—
these are taught as leading to the non-reality of Bodhisattvas; conversely, for those who apply themselves [to practice], they are taught as leading to that reality.
For by means of the secondary aids such as generosity and the rest, the wise ones indeed discipline sentient beings throughout all the stages, removing the sixfold class of opposing factors.
The prophecy for the wise is twofold, according to the distinction of time and person;
it is likewise proclaimed as being [concerned] with enlightenment, with the prophecy itself, and another which is great.

Through the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising [of phenomena], through the abandonment of pride and effortful exertion, and through attaining oneness with all the Buddhas and the Sons of the Victors; MSA 19.36.
Furthermore, that [receptacle of the Dharma] is intended by way of its field, its name, its time, its designation as a kalpa,
and its persistence through the duration of the True Dharma.

For the wise, there is the certainty of the arising of excellence, lack of weariness, constancy in cultivation, non-falling from meditative concentration, the accomplishment of tasks without effort, and the attainment of patience in every respect. (MSA 19.38)
Worship, undertaking the training, compassion, cultivation of the wholesome,
heedfulness in the forest, and likewise insatiability regarding what has been heard and its meaning—
these are the necessary duties for the wise on all stages.
Knowledge of the defects in sensual pleasures, examination of one's own transgressions,
the endurance of suffering, and the cultivation of the wholesome.
Non-indulgence in pleasure and the non-conceptualization of signs—
this is indeed what must be practiced continuously by the wise on all the stages.
The gift of Dharma, purity of ethical discipline, the very patience of non-arising,
the exertion of vigor in the Mahāyāna, the final abiding accompanied by compassion, and wisdom— these are considered the primary [perfections] among the pāramitās by the wise. (MSA 19.42)
The establishment of the fields of knowledge according to the distinctions of form, such as the Sūtras and so forth,
should be understood by the wise as the establishment of the Dharma on all the stages.
Furthermore, the establishment of sentient beings is sevenfold based on suchness;
likewise, the establishment of reasoning and vehicles is fourfold and threefold respectively.
Proper mental attention, right view accompanied by its fruit, investigation through the means of valid cognition, and the inconceivable object of knowledge—this is the fourfold reasoning. (MSA 19.45)
The vehicle is held to be threefold due to differences in intention, teaching, application, equipment, and full realization. (MSA 19.46)

The investigation into the adventitious nature of both name and object with respect to one another, and the investigation into the fact that the two kinds of designation therein consist of nothing more than that [designation]. (MSA 19.47)
And because of the non-apprehension of everything, the fourfold knowledge of reality arises for the wise on all the stages for the sake of accomplishing all goals.
For the sign (nimitta) is indeed the seed of bondage, consisting of the basis, the enjoyment, and the seed itself;
it is the mind and mental factors, together with their support and their seeds, that are bound therein. (MSA 19.49)
The wise one, by thoroughly discerning every sign— both that which is placed before him and that which exists of its own accord— attains supreme enlightenment.

The wisdom that has suchness as its object, which is free from the grasping of duality and directly perceives the body of coarse wickedness, is held by the wise to be [the knowledge] for its destruction.
Knowledge that has suchness as its object, cultivated without diverse aspects,
is said to be direct perception regarding the reality of existence and non-existence, and to be sovereign over conceptual construction.
Having concealed reality, unreality appears everywhere to the foolish; but for Bodhisattvas, having discarded that [unreality], reality appears everywhere.
The non-appearance of the unreal object and the appearance of the real object should be understood [respectively];
that transformation of the basis is liberation, because of the attainment of mastery over one's desires.
Mutually similar, appearing as a great object everywhere, it is an obstacle; therefore, having fully understood this, one should abandon it.

That which is to be matured, that which is to be purified, that which is to be attained, and that which is suitable for maturation—these objects of correct teaching are indeed immeasurable for the wise. (MSA 19.56)
The arising of the bodhisattva-mind and the very patience regarding non-arising; the stainless eye and the inferior [eye], as well as the destruction of the outflows.

The long endurance of the true Dharma, the development of understanding, the severing of doubts, and the enjoyment [of the Dharma]—these should be known as the fruits for the wise one who is devoted to teaching. (MSA 19.58)
There is the greatness of the object, as well as that of the two types of practice, of knowledge, of the exertion of vigor, and of skill in means. (MSA 19.59)
The greatness of its realization and the greatness of the Buddha’s activity— indeed, because of its connection with these two forms of greatness, it is designated as the "Great Vehicle" (Mahāyāna).
The lineage, resolute belief in the Dharma, the generation of the thought of enlightenment, the practice of giving and so forth, and likewise the entry into the right method; MSA 19.61.
The ripening of sentient beings, the purification of the field, non-abiding nirvana, and supreme enlightenment through vision. (MSA 19.62)
One is characterized by resolute belief, and another by pure high resolve;
there are also those who practice with signs, without signs, and without effort—
these five types of bodhisattvas are to be known throughout all the stages.

One who is unattached to sensual pleasures, whose threefold actions are pure, who has overcome anger, who is devoted to virtuous qualities, who is immovable in the Dharma, whose vision penetrates the profound reality, and who truly yearns for enlightenment— such a one is indeed a bodhisattva.

Desiring to favor others, viewing them without malice, and enduring injuries from others; steadfast, vigilant, and learned—one who is thus devoted to the welfare of others is indeed a bodhisattva. (MSA 19.65)

A Bodhisattva is indeed one who recognizes the peril in his own possessions, is unattached to enjoyments, does not conceal his enmity, is skilled in signs, is free from wrong views, and is established within the inner self. (MSA 19.66)
Endowed with compassion, established in the quality of moral shame, enduring suffering and unattached to his own pleasures,
preeminent in mindfulness and with a well-composed mind, the Bodhisattva is indeed unshakeable in his vehicle.

The Bodhisattva indeed endures suffering: he removes suffering and yet does not cause suffering; he dwells with suffering and yet is not afraid of suffering; he is liberated from suffering and yet does not conceptualize it as suffering. MSA 19.68.

Delighting in the Dharma and not delighting in what is non-Dharma, naturally repulsed by what is non-Dharma, and devoted to the Dharma; having mastery over the Dharma, free from the darkness regarding the Dharma, and making the Dharma his primary concern—such indeed is a Bodhisattva. (MSA 19.69)

The Bodhisattva is indeed vigilant regarding enjoyments, vigilant regarding observances, vigilant regarding protection, vigilant regarding the wholesome, vigilant regarding happiness, vigilant regarding the Dharma, and vigilant regarding the vehicle. (MSA 19.70)

The Bodhisattva indeed possesses shame regarding contempt, shame regarding slight faults, shame regarding impatience, shame regarding decline, shame regarding extensive distraction, shame regarding narrow vision, and shame regarding other vehicles. (MSA 19.71)
In this world and in the next, through equanimity, through the application of formative forces, through the attainment of masteries,
and through the teaching of tranquility and peace that yields great fruit, the bodhisattva abides in beneficial assistance.
The Bodhisattva, the Mahāsattva, the wise one of supreme splendor;
the Son of the Victor, the Support of the Victor, the Conqueror, and the Sprout of the Victor.
He is valiant, most wonderful, a caravan leader of great renown;
he is compassionate, of great merit, a lord, and likewise righteous.
Because of his awakening to the state of being a *suta* (hearer), his awakening to the great purpose, his awakening to all objects, and his constant awakening;
and because of his awakening to skillful means—by virtue of that distinction, he is called a *bodhisattva*.
Because of the awakening to the self, the awakening to the subtle view, the awakening to manifold representations,
and the awakening to all unreal conceptualization— for these reasons, one is called a bodhisattva.
Because of the awakening to non-awakening, the awakening to subsequent awakening, the awakening to non-existence, the awakening to origination,
and the awakening to the realization of non-awakening— for these reasons he is called a *bodhisattva*.
Because of the awakening to what is not an object, the awakening to the ultimate object, the awakening to all objects, the awakening to every object,
and the awakening to the awakening that is the basis for the awakening to what is to be awakened— by this reason he is called a *bodhisattva*.
