Because of the awakening to perfection, the awakening to the [three] stages, and the awakening to the womb; because of the awakening to the sequential manifestation and the awakening that utterly eliminates doubt—for these reasons, one is called a *bodhisattva*.
The wise one is indeed a possessor [of gains] and a non-possessor, established in intelligence; he is a knower, a follower-knower, and an instructor.
His intellect is beyond verbal expression; he is both one who has destroyed pride and one who appears proud; his mind is both immature and fully matured.
The chapter on Qualities (Guṇādhikāra) [the nineteenth] in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra is completed.
The twentieth and twenty-first chapters,
concerning the Analysis of Marks (Liṅgavibhāga), consist of two verses.
Compassion, pleasant speech, steadfastness, open-handed generosity, and the unraveling of profound intentional meanings—these are the marks of the wise. (MSA 20.1)
The five signs are to be understood as: embracing [the teaching], attaining resolute faith, being untiring, the twofold gathering [of disciples], and both intention and application. (MSA 20.2)
For Bodhisattvas, constantly becoming universal monarchs (cakravartin),
indeed accomplish the welfare of sentient beings as householders throughout all their births.
The going forth obtained through formal adoption is supreme as it accords with the nature of reality;
and for the wise, this going forth serves as a demonstration throughout all the stages.
The side of the one who has gone forth is endowed with immeasurable qualities;
for this reason, the ascetic is superior to the householder bodhisattva.
The wise ones' intention toward sentient beings is held to be the desire for their desired results in the next world, the desire for virtuous conduct in this very life, and the desire for nirvāṇa;
it is impure, pure, and utterly pure throughout all the stages.
For the wise, on all the stages, there is the embracing [of beings] through their vow, through an even mind, through sovereignty, and through the drawing together of the assembly.
The birth of the wise is considered to arise through the sovereignty of karma, as well as through that of aspiration, meditative concentration, and mastery. (MSA 20.8)

The dwelling and the stage itself are established by way of their characteristics, the person, the training, the accomplishment of the aggregates, the signs, the etymology, and the attainment. (MSA 20.9)
Emptiness is the supreme self; there is the establishment of the non-destruction of karma.
Having dwelt in meditative absorptions accompanied by bliss, thereafter [there is] birth in the desire realm.
And then there is the dedication of the factors conducive to enlightenment toward cyclic existence,
and the maturation of sentient beings without mental affliction.
Furthermore, there is the intentional preservation of affliction for the sake of rebirth;
this is the path exclusively devoted to the signless, which adheres to the single way.
Even in the signless state there is effortlessness, the purification of the field, and the perfection of the ripening of sentient beings; and beyond that, [the ultimate fruit] arises.
The purity of the concentrations, the dhāraṇīs, and of awakening itself—
through this systematic arrangement, the characteristic of the stages is to be understood.
Possessing pure vision and perfectly purified ethical discipline, concentrated, and with pride dispelled regarding the Dharma;
he has attained awakening in a single moment regarding the distinctions between the continuity [of the mind], its affliction, and its purification, as well as regarding emanation.
Equanimous, a purifier of the field, skilled in maturing sentient beings, and possessed of great supernatural power;
with a perfected body and capable of manifestation—such indeed is the consecrated Bodhisattva.
In this world, one penetrates the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) through training in higher ethics, higher mind, and higher wisdom; yet wisdom has two spheres of activity.
The reality of phenomena, as well as the mental activity consisting of the ignorance and knowledge thereof, is the domain of wisdom; therefore, its establishment occurs on two stages.
Furthermore, there is another fourfold fruit of the trainings and of cultivation:
the first fruit is the dwelling that is signless yet accompanied by effort.
That very absence of volitional effort is held to be the second fruit,
as well as the purification of the field and the ripening and perfection of sentient beings.
And the perfection of meditative concentrations and mnemonic formulas is the supreme fruit;
for these four kinds of fruits are based upon the four stages.
Having realized the true nature of phenomena here, there is the purification of the aggregate of ethical discipline;
thereafter follows the purification of the aggregates of concentration and wisdom.
In the other [stages], there is the purification of the knowledge of liberation and the knowledge of that liberation from four kinds of obscurations and also from the obscuration of resistance.
All the stages (bhūmis) should be understood as both unperfected and perfected;
furthermore, even those that are perfected are considered to be both unperfected and perfected.

Accomplishment is to be understood through mental attention according to the established order, through the knowledge that it is a conceptual construction, and through non-conceptualization of that very [construction]. (MSA 20.25)
The accomplishment of cultivation on all stages is also inconceivable,
because it is to be personally realized within oneself and because it is the domain of the Buddhas.
For resolute belief (adhimukti) is held to be the sign [of the bodhisattva] everywhere;
it is characterized by lack of despondency, lack of dejection, and the state of not being dependent on others.
Pervasive penetration, equanimity toward all,
being unswayed by or attached to anything, knowledge of skillful means, and birth within the mandala.

One who has taken refuge in a true friend is neither lacking in aspiration nor greedy and small-hearted; neither wrathful nor lazy; neither devoid of a mind of loving-kindness and compassion nor possessed of evil intellect ruined by conceptual constructions and discursive thoughts; neither distracted in mind nor overcome by pleasures, nor turned back by sufferings; such a person is devoted to hearing the Dharma and devoted to honoring the Teacher. (MSA 20.29)

Having performed a vast accumulation of all merit and dedicated it toward perfect enlightenment in common with others, he who knows the supreme means is born always in a favorable state as a doer of good; sporting with the qualities of the superknowledges, standing above all, he should be known as a treasury of virtues whose very nature is that of a Buddha. (MSA 20.30)
In both calm abiding and insight, the benefit for the wise is considered to consist of two groups of five, in every respect and on all stages.
For those seeing that enlightenment is near and that the welfare of sentient beings is being accomplished, an intense joy arises; therefore, it is called "Joy" (muditā).

The stage is called *vimalā* (the Stainless) because it is free from the impurity of the exertion toward misconduct; and it is called *prabhākarī* (the Radiant) because it produces the great illumination of the Dharma.

Since the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) have become like flames and are thus incandescent, that stage is called "The Radiant" (*Arciṣmatī*) because of its connection with them, due to the burning away of duality.
Because the wise endure suffering for the sake of maturing sentient beings and protecting their own minds, this stage is called "Difficult to Conquer" (Durjayā).
Because it faces both cyclic existence and nirvana here,
this stage is called "The Facing" (Abhimukhī), owing to its reliance upon the perfection of wisdom.
The stage is considered "Far-reaching" (Dūramgamā) due to its connection with the single path;
it is designated as "Immovable" (Acalā) because of the lack of movement caused by the two types of perception.
Because of the excellence of the intellect consisting of the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), this stage is considered Sādhumatī ("Good Intelligence").
Dharmameghā ("Dharma-Cloud") is so called because it pervades the two [aspects] like a cloud in the sky of the Dharma.
Because they always dwell with delight in the various accomplishments of the auspicious,
the stages of dwelling of the bodhisattvas are considered to exist everywhere.
Because they involve ascending higher and higher through these immeasurable stages,
and because they serve the purpose of bringing immeasurable beings to freedom from fear, these very stages are indeed desired.
It is fourfold: through the attainment of the stages, through resolute belief, through proceeding in the practices, and through the penetration and the perfection of the stages.

For the sake of attracting those embodied beings who have faith in the Mahāyāna and those in the Hīnayāna, and for their discipline, the four practices of the wise have been taught according to the sūtras. (MSA 20.42)
Homage be to you, who have compassion for sentient beings, whose intention is their union [with happiness] and separation [from suffering],
whose intention is their non-separation [from happiness], and whose intention is their welfare and bliss.
O Sage, liberated from all obscurations, who has surpassed the entire world; O you whose mind is liberated, your knowable object is pervaded by your wisdom—homage be to you!
O destroyer of all afflictions of all sentient beings without exception, O striker down of the afflictions, you who possess compassion even for those afflicted— homage be to you!
Effortless, unattached, unimpeded, and ever concentrated—you who always provide answers to all questions, homage be to you! (MSA 20.46)
O Excellent Teacher, whose wisdom is ever unimpeded regarding the basis and that which is based upon it, as well as the teaching and the knowledge that guides— it is to you that I pay homage.
Having approached them with words suited to their conduct, you know their coming and going, as well as the lack of essence in sentient beings; homage be to you, the perfect instructor! MSA 20.48.
Upon seeing you, all embodied beings attain the state of true manhood;
homage be to you, who bestow grace at the mere sight of you! (MSA 20.49)
Homage be to you who have attained mastery over concentration and wisdom regarding taking up, maintaining, relinquishing, creating, and transforming.
Homage be to you, the crusher of Māra, who dispels the delusions of sentient beings regarding the means, the refuge, purity, the Mahāyāna, and the departure [from saṃsāra]. MSA_20.51.
O Teacher who reveals knowledge, abandonment, liberation, and the obstacles thereto;
you who are invincible to other sectarians in the pursuit of the welfare of yourself and others—homage be to you!
One who speaks with restraint in assemblies, free from the two types of affliction, without need for protection, unerring, and a leader of the community—homage be to you! (MSA 20.53)
In movement and in rest, everywhere there is no conduct that is not that of an omniscient one;
O Omniscient One, you who always perceive the true nature of reality, homage be to you! (MSA 20.54)
In all activities for the benefit of sentient beings, you do not let the proper time pass;
your deeds are always fruitful and you are never forgetful—homage be to you! (MSA 20.55)
Six times throughout every day and night, you survey the entire world;
endowed with great compassion and intent upon the welfare [of others], homage be to you!
Through your conduct, your realization, your wisdom, and your activity— you who are supreme among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas— homage be to you!
O you who have attained great enlightenment in all its aspects through the three bodies,
who cuts through the doubts of all sentient beings everywhere— homage be to you!
Unrestrained, faultless, stainless, and non-abiding;
unmoving amidst all phenomena and free from conceptual proliferation—homage be to you!
You have perfected the ultimate truth and have emerged from all the stages;
you have attained supremacy among all sentient beings and are the liberator of all sentient beings.
Endowed with inexhaustible and incomparable qualities, you appear in the worlds;
yet within the maṇḍalas as well, you are entirely invisible to gods and humans alike.
In the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, spoken by the Great Bodhisattva Vyavadātasamaya, the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Foundation of Conduct," is completed;
and thus the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* is finished.
